structured_output.summary: Wrote the complete first draft of the application for the passive cold-chain carrier: all ten body sections in draft/, the reference-numeral table, and five figure specifications (whole-carrier section, thermal module perspective, lid-registration detail, condensate detail, exposure-indicator detail). Claim 1 recites the lid-registered passive circulation path around the suspended perforated tray and opposed cassettes; independent claims also cover the thermal module alone and the method of transporting. prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so the Background carries no citations and the art available to this draft may be incomplete.
reasoning: Claim 1 was built around the one relationship the disclosure calls essential: the registered circulation path (centre rise, split along opposed cassette faces, descend outboard guide ducts, cross the side supply passages and tray perforations, return beneath the tray) combined with a lid-carried depending indexing rib that enters a mating channel of the spacer frame and shifts the module until the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages. Registration does technical work rather than being decorative: it is what makes the flow geometry independent of how the packer set the module down, and the Background and Detailed Description state that problem and that effect expressly so a later argument has something in the specification to stand on.

The negative recitation that the carrier is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover stayed in claim 1. The inventor states passivity as the character of the invention, and it is the limitation that keeps the claim off forced-air shippers, which is the family a claim to ducted airflow around a payload would otherwise read onto.

Everything the disclosure marks optional was kept out of claim 1 and put on the ladder instead: retention of the module by resilient feet pressed onto shell ledges (claim 2, the next-narrowest fallback because it comes from the same closing movement), the compressible lid gasket sealing after registration (claims 3 and 4), the cassette and duct geometry (claims 5 and 6), the perforation placement (claim 7), condensate channel, wick, discharge openings and pull tab (claims 8 to 10), and the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator (claims 11 to 14). Each of those is a feature that could be argued on its own.

Three statutory classes are covered because different parties infringe them: the carrier as a whole (claim 1), the thermal module alone (claim 16, aimed at a module or cassette-kit supplier, reciting the mating channel positioned to be entered by the lid rib so that the module is shifted into the registered position), and a method of transporting temperature-sensitive goods (claim 20, aimed at the packer and shipper, including the closing step that performs registration).

prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references at all, so there was nothing to read around, nothing to cite, and no reference-specific clearing argument to make. The Background is therefore written from the general problem (stratification and shipment-to-shipment variability in passive carriers, alignment lost at the packing bench, condensate on repeated reuse, and the fact that a recovered refrigerant leaves no trace of an excursion) without characterising any document.

Two details the disclosure does not supply were written as supported functional language rather than invented structure. An earlier dependent claim to downwardly converging channel surfaces was removed and the description now says only that the mating channel and the entering rib are shaped so that engagement during the closing travel translates the frame horizontally. The exposed position of the indicator stem is described as projecting beyond, or presenting a contrasting portion at, the outer surface of the shell, with the projecting variant used for the drawing.

Figure work was split into five sheets rather than crowded onto three: eight numerals is the ceiling, and the module, the lid-registration interface, the condensate path and the indicator are at four different locations and scales. Where a body appears on a sheet only as context, it is described generically without its canonical part name so no sheet shows a named part it does not list; that is why the shell wall in FIG. 4 and the lid in FIG. 3 are described as an insulating wall body and a closure slab.

The Detailed Description pairs a numeral with a FIG. reference only where that numeral is listed on that sheet, so the guide ducts are pointed to FIG. 4 (where their lower ends and discharge openings appear) rather than to FIG. 2, and the ledge and resilient foot relationship is pointed to FIG. 3.

The Background accordingly contains no citations of any kind, and no reference is characterised anywhere in the draft. In place of reference-specific differentiation, claim 1 was drawn to the relationship the disclosure identifies as essential and expressed in terms that are concrete and cooperative rather than generic: not merely a cold source above a payload with air gaps, but a spacer frame whose central inlet takes the rising stream, splits it along the confronting faces of two opposed cassettes, sends it down guide ducts outboard of those cassettes to peripheral outlets that overlap side supply passages formed between the tray and shell walls, through tray perforations and back beneath a tray suspended on feet, with the overlap itself created by a depending lid rib entering a channel in the frame as the lid closes and with no powered air mover anywhere. structured_output.answer:
The full application is written. draft/ now holds the title, cross-reference and government-support statements (both Not applicable, per the filing notes), field, background, summary, brief description of the drawings, detailed description, 23 claims, abstract, and the reference-numeral table. figures/ holds five self-contained drawing specifications.

Claim 1 is the carrier: an insulated outer shell; a product tray on tray feet leaving a lower return passage, its side walls spaced inward from the shell side walls to form two side supply passages, with perforations through the tray; a thermal module comprising a rigid spacer frame and two opposed phase-change cassettes, the frame defining a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes, peripheral outlet openings at the duct lower ends, and a mating channel; and an insulated lid whose depending indexing rib enters that channel as the lid closes and shifts the module into a registered position in which the outlet openings overlap the side supply passages. The claim closes with the carrier being free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover, and with the four bodies cooperating in the registered position to define the circulation path: rise from the product region into the central inlet, split along the cassette faces, descend the guide ducts, enter the side supply passages, pass the perforations, return beneath the tray.

The optional features are on the dependent ladder rather than in claim 1: ledge-and-resilient-foot retention (claim 2), the gasket sealing after registration (claims 3 and 4), cassette and duct geometry (claims 5 and 6), perforation placement (claim 7), the condensate channel, wick, discharge openings and pull tab (claims 8 to 10), and the irreversible exposure indicator including its latched exposed position, manual reset after opening, and non-interference with airflow (claims 11 to 14). Claim 16 covers the thermal module alone and claim 20 the method of transporting, so a module supplier and a packer are reached by different claims.

Two details the disclosure does not supply are written as functional language rather than invented structure: the rib and channel are described only as shaped so that engagement during the closing travel translates the frame horizontally, and the indicator's exposed position is described as projecting beyond, or presenting a contrasting portion at, the outer surface of the shell.

One thing to flag: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references. The Background therefore cites nothing, and no clearing argument could be made against real documents. As the brief anticipated, the art available to this draft may be incomplete, and the claims should be tested against a search before filing.

The abstract (141 words) matches claim 1. numerals.md is complete and one-to-one with the description; no drafting notes, placeholders or open questions remain anywhere in draft/ or figures/.

24 findings are reported. The critical ones are untraced technical matter:

1. Material and construction menus invented by the drafter - insulating materials for shell and lid ("moulded expanded polymer, a vacuum insulated panel assembly, a rigid polyurethane foam core within a moulded skin"), tray-foot forms, resilient-foot materials, wick materials, and perforation forms. The disclosure names none of these; it says only "insulated outer shell", "feet", "resilient feet", "absorbent wick", "perforations".

2. Cassette internal construction ("a sealed rigid container charged with a phase-change material") - the disclosure says only "phase-change cassettes".

3. A new non-contact cooling relationship - "The spacer frame 42 holds the phase-change cassettes clear of the product tray 20, so that goods ... are not in contact with a cassette surface" - carried into claim 6. The disclosure says only that the frame "rests above the product tray".

- fig-01 places 10 and 100 on the same shell body.

Formalities: FIGS. 1, 3, 4 and 5 are sectional views with no section line and no source view designating the cutting plane, and FIGS. 3-5 are not tied to FIG. 1; the title departs from the brief's working title; claim 21 and the Brief Description say "lid gasket" where the description and numerals say "compressible lid gasket 64".

No patentability, novelty, validity or prior-art-tracing assessment was performed, and rendered images were not inspected.

input.content:
In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.

The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12.

The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. The tray side walls 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.

The thermal module

Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by a given payload are fitted before packing and exchanged between shipments.

The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, located beside the phase-change cassettes, each guide duct 50 lying outboard of an outer face of one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame 42, each peripheral outlet opening 54 being at a lower end of one of the guide ducts 50.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58 at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame 42. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 that extends around the underside of the insulated lid 60 outboard of the depending indexing rib 62. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 need only be dropped into the outer shell 10 approximately, and may be set down offset or skewed within the clearance available to it. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is then created by closing the lid, which is an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 project inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10 beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. The resilient feet 58 maintain a downward holding force during transport, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.

The circulation path

In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the confronting inner faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams that travel outward over the cassette faces. Each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Circulation is driven by the density difference between air warmed in the product region and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes. The geometry supports that difference rather than substituting for it: the cooled air is produced at the top of the carrier and is given a continuous downward path of its own along the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, while the warmed air is given a continuous upward path through the product region to the central inlet opening 48, and the two paths meet only at the central inlet opening 48 and beneath the product tray 20. Because the supply and return legs are separated by the tray side walls 26 rather than sharing one opening, the descending cooled stream is not obliged to pass through the ascending warmed stream.

Condensate management

A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough that extends around the product tray 20 at a lower region of the outer shell 10, beneath the side supply passages 28. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70. Discharge openings 76, separate from the peripheral outlet openings 54, are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

Mechanical exposure indicator

Referring to FIG. 6, the outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44 when the thermal module 40 is in the registered position.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again and the temperature-responsive latch 84 has returned to its retaining condition, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.

Operation

In use, phase-change cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by the payload are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. Goods are placed in the product tray 20 and the product tray 20 is placed in the outer shell 10 so that the tray feet 22 stand on the floor 12, leaving the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20 and the two side supply passages 28 between the tray side walls 26 and the side walls 14. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20. The insulated lid 60 is then closed, whereby the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 and shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position, the resilient feet 58 are pressed against the ledges 18 to retain the thermal module 40, and the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. Air thereafter circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover. At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.

Alternatives

Two phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42, opposed across the central space. Entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.

The described implementations are examples. A person skilled in the art may combine, substitute or omit the described features within the scope of the claims that follow.

The geometry supports that difference rather than substituting for it: the cooled air is produced at the top of the carrier and is given a continuous downward path of its own along the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, while the warmed air is given a continuous upward path through the product region to the central inlet opening 48, and the two paths meet only at the central inlet opening 48 and beneath the product tray 20. Because the supply and return legs are separated by the tray side walls 26 rather than sharing one opening, the descending cooled stream is not obliged to pass through the ascending warmed stream.

Condensate management

A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough that extends around the product tray 20 at a lower region of the outer shell 10, beneath the side supply passages 28. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70. Discharge openings 76, separate from the peripheral outlet openings 54, are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

Mechanical exposure indicator

Referring to FIG. 6, the outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44 when the thermal module 40 is in the registered position.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again and the temperature-responsive latch 84 has returned to its retaining condition, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.

Operation

In use, phase-change cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by the payload are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. Goods are placed in the product tray 20 and the product tray 20 is placed in the outer shell 10 so that the tray feet 22 stand on the floor 12, leaving the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20 and the two side supply passages 28 between the tray side walls 26 and the side walls 14. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20. The insulated lid 60 is then closed, whereby the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 and shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position, the resilient feet 58 are pressed against the ledges 18 to retain the thermal module 40, and the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. Air thereafter circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover. At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.

Alternatives

Two phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42, opposed across the central space. Entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.

The described implementations are examples. A person skilled in the art may combine, substitute or omit the described features within the scope of the claims that follow.

Mechanical exposure indicator

Referring to FIG. 5, the outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes a body received in the outer shell 10, an indicator stem 82 movable in the body between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The body of the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is seated in a bore through a wall of the outer shell 10 and has an internal shoulder, the spring 86 acting between that internal shoulder and a collar on the indicator stem 82, and the temperature-responsive latch 84 being carried by the body and engaging the indicator stem 82. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44, an inner end region of the indicator stem 82 lying against or in conductive contact with the first phase-change cassette 44 when the thermal module 40 is in the registered position.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens, that is, when the phase-change material of that cassette has passed out of the state in which it holds the payload at temperature. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10. In some implementations the exposed position is one in which an outer end portion of the indicator stem 82 projects beyond an outer surface of the outer shell 10; in others it is one in which a contrasting portion of the indicator stem 82 is presented at the outer surface.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again and the temperature-responsive latch 84 has returned to its retaining condition, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.

Operation

In use, phase-change cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by the payload are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. Goods are placed in the product tray 20 and the product tray 20 is placed in the outer shell 10 so that the tray feet 22 stand on the floor 12, leaving the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20 and the two side supply passages 28 between the tray side walls 26 and the side walls 14. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20. The insulated lid 60 is then closed, whereby the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 and shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position, the resilient feet 58 are pressed against the ledges 18 to retain the thermal module 40, and the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. Air thereafter circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover. At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.

Alternatives

The number of phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42 is two in the described arrangement, the two being opposed across the central space so that each face of the rising stream is cooled symmetrically. The mating channel 56 and the depending indexing rib 62 may be interchanged in the sense that the channel may be longer than the rib or the rib longer than the channel, provided that entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 may be continuous slots along the outboard lower regions of the spacer frame 42 or a series of discrete openings, provided that they overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.

The described implementations are examples. A person skilled in the art may combine, substitute or omit the described features within the scope of the claims that follow.

An upright rectangular container occupies the centre of the drawing area: a thick hatched left wall body and a thick hatched right wall body of equal height, joined at the bottom by a thick hatched horizontal bottom body. A passive cold-chain carrier is disclosed in which the closing of the lid, rather than the care of the packer, establishes the circulation path.

In one aspect, the carrier includes an insulated outer shell having a floor and side walls, a product tray removably received in the outer shell, a thermal module removably received in the outer shell above the product tray, and an insulated lid. The product tray is supported above the floor by tray feet so that a lower return passage remains between the product tray and the floor, and the tray side walls are spaced inward from the side walls of the outer shell to form two side supply passages. The thermal module includes a rigid spacer frame and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame, the spacer frame defining a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings. The insulated lid carries a depending indexing rib positioned to enter a mating channel of the spacer frame as the lid closes and to shift the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages.

In the registered position the shell, the product tray, the thermal module and the lid cooperate to define a circulation path along which air rising from a product region within the product tray enters the central inlet opening, divides along faces of the two phase-change cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage. The carrier is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover, and the circulation is driven by the density difference between the air warmed in the product region and the air cooled along the cassette faces.

The technical effect of lid-driven registration is that the alignment on which the circulation path depends is created by an act the packer cannot omit. The thermal module may be dropped into the outer shell approximately, offset or skewed, and the depending indexing rib entering the mating channel translates the module into the position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages. The seal made by a compressible lid gasket against the upper edge of the outer shell occurs after registration, so the carrier is not closed against a module that is still out of position. The same closing movement presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the outer shell, so that the registered module is held down against the product tray and cannot lift away from it under the vibration and inversion of transport.

In a further aspect, a shallow condensate channel extends around the product tray and receives a removable absorbent wick. Discharge openings at lower ends of the guide ducts deliver condensate that forms on the cassettes into the condensate channel. A pull tab on the absorbent wick remains accessible when the product tray is removed, so the wick is replaced without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service.

In a further aspect, the outer shell carries a mechanical exposure indicator visible from outside the carrier. An indicator stem is thermally coupled to one of the phase-change cassettes and is retained by a temperature-responsive latch. If that cassette softens enough to release the latch, a spring moves the indicator stem to a latched exposed position, and the indication remains exposed after the cassette cools again, being reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The indicator therefore reports the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends, survives recovery of the cassette, and requires no battery. The exposure indicator does not control airflow, so the circulation path is unaffected by whether the indicator has tripped.

In a further aspect, a method includes fitting conditioned phase-change cassettes to the spacer frame, placing product in the product tray, placing the product tray in the outer shell, placing the thermal module above the product tray, and closing the insulated lid so that the depending indexing rib enters the mating channel and shifts the thermal module into the registered position, whereafter air circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover.

The features summarised above may be used together or separately, and the summary is not a statement of the scope of the claims.

In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.

The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12.

The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. The tray side walls 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.

The thermal module

Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by a given payload are fitted before packing and exchanged between shipments.

The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, located beside the phase-change cassettes, each guide duct 50 lying outboard of an outer face of one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame 42, each peripheral outlet opening 54 being at a lower end of one of the guide ducts 50.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58 at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame 42. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 that extends around the underside of the insulated lid 60 outboard of the depending indexing rib 62. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 need only be dropped into the outer shell 10 approximately, and may be set down offset or skewed within the clearance available to it. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is then created by closing the lid, which is an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 project inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10 beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. The resilient feet 58 maintain a downward holding force during transport, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.

The circulation path

In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the confronting inner faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams that travel outward over the cassette faces. Each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Circulation is driven by the density difference between air warmed in the product region and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes. The geometry supports that difference rather than substituting for it: the cooled air is produced at the top of the carrier and is given a continuous downward path of its own along the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, while the warmed air is given a continuous upward path through the product region to the central inlet opening 48, and the two paths meet only at the central inlet opening 48 and beneath the product tray 20. Because the supply and return legs are separated by the tray side walls 26 rather than sharing one opening, the descending cooled stream is not obliged to pass through the ascending warmed stream.

Condensate management

A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough that extends around the product tray 20 at a lower region of the outer shell 10, beneath the side supply passages 28. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70. Discharge openings 76, separate from the peripheral outlet openings 54, are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

Mechanical exposure indicator

Referring to FIG. 6, the outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44 when the thermal module 40 is in the registered position.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again and the temperature-responsive latch 84 has returned to its retaining condition, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.

Operation

In use, phase-change cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by the payload are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. Goods are placed in the product tray 20 and the product tray 20 is placed in the outer shell 10 so that the tray feet 22 stand on the floor 12, leaving the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20 and the two side supply passages 28 between the tray side walls 26 and the side walls 14. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20. The insulated lid 60 is then closed, whereby the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 and shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position, the resilient feet 58 are pressed against the ledges 18 to retain the thermal module 40, and the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. Air thereafter circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover. At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.

Alternatives

Two phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42, opposed across the central space. Entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.

The described implementations are examples. A person skilled in the art may combine, substitute or omit the described features within the scope of the claims that follow.

# FIG. 1

## View
Schematic vertical sectional view of an assembled passive cold-chain carrier, seen horizontally. Plain black line work on white, diagonal section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

## Geometry to draw
An upright rectangular container occupies the centre of the drawing area: a thick hatched left wall body and a thick hatched right wall body, joined at the bottom by a thick hatched horizontal bottom body. These form the sectioned outer shell 10, whose bottom body is the floor 12. The container is open at the top.

A thick hatched horizontal slab lies across the top ends of both wall bodies, spanning the full outer width, its underside overlying the top ends of both wall bodies. This slab is the insulated lid 60, closed. The gasket interface at those top ends is shown enlarged in FIG. 3.

Inside the container, a sectioned open-top box is drawn with thin hatched walls: an upright left wall, an upright right wall and a horizontal bottom wall joining them. This box is the product tray 20. Its bottom wall is raised above the top surface of the floor 12, and its outer side surfaces stand clear of the inner surfaces of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap on each side running from the top of the box down to the floor 12.

Two short hatched blocks stand between the underside of the tray bottom wall and the top surface of the floor 12, one near each end of the tray. These blocks are the tray feet 22. The open horizontal space between that underside and that top surface, extending between and beyond the blocks, is the lower return passage 24.

In the upper interior, between the inner surfaces of the two wall bodies and between the open top of the product tray 20 and the underside of the insulated lid 60, a horizontally elongated hatched body is drawn in section. This body is the thermal module 40. Two upright plain rectangular blocks are drawn within it, shown schematically, spaced from one another and from its outboard ends. The hatched body is open downward at its centre between those blocks, and an open vertical channel runs down through it outboard of each block, opening through its outboard side above the vertical gap beside the product tray 20.

## Reference numerals on this sheet
10, 12, 20, 22, 24, 40, 60, 100

## Numeral targets
- 10: well inside the hatching of the left wall body.
- 12: well inside the hatching of the bottom body.
- 20: well inside the left upright wall of the open-top box.
- 22: well inside the left short block on the floor.
- 24: inside the open space between the tray bottom wall and the floor.
- 40: well inside the elongated upper body, clear of the upright blocks.
- 60: well inside the horizontal slab at the top.
- 100: outside the container, clear of all line work, with a lead line ending in an arrow directed at the assembled carrier as a whole.

# FIG. 1

## View
Schematic vertical sectional view of an assembled passive cold-chain carrier, seen horizontally. Plain black line work on white, section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

## Geometry to draw
An upright rectangular container occupies the centre of the drawing area: a thick hatched left wall body and a thick hatched right wall body, joined at the bottom by a thick hatched horizontal bottom body. These form the sectioned outer shell 10, whose bottom body is the floor 12. The container is open at the top.

A thick hatched horizontal slab lies across the top ends of both wall bodies, spanning the full outer width and overlying those top ends. This slab is the insulated lid 60, closed. The gasket interface at those top ends is shown enlarged in FIG. 3.

Inside the container, a sectioned open-top box is drawn with thin hatched walls: an upright left wall, an upright right wall and a horizontal bottom wall joining them. This box is the product tray 20. Its bottom wall is raised above the top surface of the floor 12, and its outer side surfaces stand clear of the inner surfaces of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap on each side running from the top of the box down to the floor 12.

Two short hatched blocks stand between the underside of the tray bottom wall and the top surface of the floor 12, one near each end of the tray. These blocks are the tray feet 22. The open horizontal space between that underside and that top surface is the lower return passage 24.

In the upper interior, between the open top of the product tray 20 and the underside of the insulated lid 60, a horizontally elongated hatched body is drawn in section. This body is the thermal module 40. Two upright plain rectangular blocks are drawn within it, shown schematically, spaced from one another and from its outboard ends. The hatched body is open downward at its centre between those blocks, and an open vertical channel runs down through it outboard of each block, opening through its outboard side above the vertical gap beside the product tray 20.

## Reference numerals on this sheet
10, 12, 20, 22, 24, 40, 60, 100

## Numeral targets
- 10: well inside the hatching of the left wall body.
- 12: well inside the hatching of the bottom body.
- 20: well inside the left upright wall of the open-top box.
- 22: well inside the left short block on the floor.
- 24: inside the open space between the tray bottom wall and the floor.
- 40: well inside the elongated upper body, clear of the upright blocks.
- 60: well inside the horizontal slab at the top.
- 100: outside the container, clear of all line work, with a lead line ending in an arrow directed at the assembled carrier as a whole.

# FIG. 4

## View
Enlarged view of a lower side region of FIG. 1, seen horizontally in section. Plain black line work on white, diagonal section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

## Geometry to draw
A thick hatched upright insulating wall body occupies the left portion of the drawing area and runs the full height of the fragment, its inner surface facing right.

In the upper right part of the drawing area, a hatched body fragment is drawn in section, representing the lower outboard region of the thermal module. Its left face is spaced from the inner surface of the upright wall body, leaving an open vertical space between them. An open vertical channel passes down through this fragment, bounded by hatched material to its left and right. This channel is one of the guide ducts 50.

At the foot of that channel, an opening passes through the left face of the body fragment, so that the channel opens sideways into the open vertical space between the fragment and the upright wall body. This opening is one of the peripheral outlet openings 54.

Below the body fragment, and spaced to the right of the inner surface of the upright wall body, a thin hatched upright wall is drawn in section and runs downward to the lower edge of the fragment. This thin wall is one of the tray side walls 26. The open vertical space continues down between the upright wall body and the thin wall, so that the space fed through the peripheral outlet opening 54 runs downward past the thin wall. This continuing space is one of the side supply passages 28.

In the lower portion of the thin wall, a series of small openings passes through it from its left surface to its right surface, shown schematically. These openings are the perforations 30.

## Reference numerals on this sheet
26, 28, 30, 50, 54

## Numeral targets
- 26: well inside the hatching of the thin upright wall, above the small openings.
- 28: inside the open vertical space between the upright wall body and the thin wall.
- 30: on one of the small openings toward the middle of the series.
- 50: inside the open vertical channel in the body fragment.
- 54: on the opening through the left face of the body fragment.

# FIG. 5

## View
Enlarged view of the condensate channel region of FIG. 1, seen horizontally in section. Plain black line work on white, diagonal section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

## Geometry to draw
A thick hatched upright insulating wall body occupies the left portion of the drawing area, running from the upper part of the fragment down to a thick hatched horizontal bottom body that occupies the lower part and extends rightward.

In the upper right part of the drawing area, a hatched body fragment is drawn in section, representing the lower outboard region of the thermal module. An open vertical channel passes down through this fragment, bounded by hatched material to its left and right. This channel is one of the guide ducts 50. At the lower end of the channel, an opening passes through the downwardly facing bottom surface of the fragment, so the channel also opens downward. This opening is one of the discharge openings 76.

Below the body fragment, a thin hatched upright wall is drawn in section, spaced to the right of the inner surface of the upright wall body and ending above the horizontal bottom body. An open vertical space runs down between the upright wall body and the thin wall, from beneath the body fragment to the horizontal bottom body, so that the downward opening in the fragment stands above that space.

In the upwardly facing top surface of the horizontal bottom body, at the foot of the open vertical space and below the discharge opening 76, a shallow upwardly open trough is drawn in section, wider than it is deep. This trough is the condensate channel 70.

An elongated body of absorbent material lies in the trough, filling its lower part, shown schematically. This body is the absorbent wick 72. A narrow strip extends upward from its upper surface into the open vertical space, its free upper end clear of the surrounding surfaces. This strip is the pull tab 74.

## Reference numerals on this sheet
50, 70, 72, 74, 76

## Numeral targets
- 50: inside the open vertical channel in the body fragment.
- 70: inside the trough at its left end, above the absorbent body.
- 72: well inside the elongated absorbent body lying in the trough.
- 74: well inside the narrow strip rising from the absorbent body.
- 76: on the opening through the bottom surface of the body fragment.

5:Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.
9:The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. The tray side walls 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.
13:Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by a given payload are fitted before packing and exchanged between shipments.
15:The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, located beside the phase-change cassettes, each guide duct 50 lying outboard of an outer face of one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame 42, each peripheral outlet opening 54 being at a lower end of one of the guide ducts 50.
21:The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 that extends around the underside of the insulated lid 60 outboard of the depending indexing rib 62. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.
25:The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 project inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10 beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. The resilient feet 58 maintain a downward holding force during transport, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.
35:A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough that extends around the product tray 20 at a lower region of the outer shell 10, beneath the side supply passages 28. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70. Discharge openings 76, separate from the peripheral outlet openings 54, are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.
41:The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. Referring to FIG. 6, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44 when the thermal module 40 is in the registered position.

content.text:
All findings are addressed. Summary of what changed:

**Untraced technical matter removed.** All material and construction menus are gone (shell and lid now read "formed of thermally insulating material"; the tray-foot, resilient-foot and wick alternative sentences are deleted). Cassette construction is now "Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material." The "holds the cassettes clear of the product tray" sentence and its no-contact effect are deleted, and claim 6 is reduced to removability of the cassettes. Perforation wall, hole shape and lengthwise distribution are deleted and the claim reciting them is cancelled. The indicator's bore, stepped shoulder, collar and latch recess are gone from both the description and the drawing brief, leaving stem, latch and spring with the indicator body shown schematically. "Conductive contact" is back to "thermally coupled" in the description and the figure, and that claim is cancelled. The two exposed-position variants, the rib/channel length variant, the outlet-opening form variant, the lower-return-passage thermal result, and the "tolerance stack of moulded insulating parts" sentence are all removed.

**Internal inconsistencies resolved.** The perforations now open from the side supply passages into the lower return passage everywhere, matching claims 1 and 18, the abstract and the disclosure. Discharge openings are recited as "separate from the peripheral outlet openings" in the description, the summary and claims 8 and 17. The air outlet is now depicted consistently: the guide duct opens through its outboard side in FIG. 1, FIG. 2 and FIG. 4. FIG. 1 now shows the lid overlying the shell top ends with that interface enlarged in FIG. 3. FIG. 6 shows the cassette confronting the stem across the intervening space. Numeral 100 now has a lead line with an arrow to the assembly, clear of the shell body.

**Figure plan.** Adding the peripheral outlet opening to the lower side region would have put nine numerals on one sheet, so that sheet was split into two focused sheets rather than dropping a part: FIG. 4 is the air path (26, 28, 30, 50, 54) and FIG. 5 the condensate path (50, 70, 72, 74, 76), with the indicator moved to FIG. 6. All 31 numerals still appear, no sheet carries more than eight, and every brief is under the character ceiling. FIG. 2's frame proportions and the four-foot count are removed; FIG. 3 no longer makes the rib integral with the lid.

**Formalities.** FIG. 1 is now a schematic sectional view, FIGS. 3, 4 and 5 are enlarged views of regions of FIG. 1, and FIG. 6 is an enlarged schematic sectional view, so no figure asserts an undesignated cutting plane. "Compressible lid gasket" is used throughout, including claim 19 and the drawing description. The title is restored to the brief's working title. Claims renumbered to 21, with dependencies referring only to claims 1, 3, 7, 10, 14 and 18.

input.summary: Fixed every finding from the source-fidelity gate. Removed all untraced technical matter (material menus, cassette construction, non-contact cooling, perforation placement and distribution, indicator internal mechanism, conductive contact, exposed-position variants, rib/channel and outlet-form variants, and two asserted performance results). Resolved the perforation flow contradiction, distinguished the discharge openings from the peripheral outlet openings, and harmonised the guide-duct air outlet, the lid-to-shell interface, the indicator geometry and the numeral 100 target across the drawings. Split the overcrowded lower-side sheet into a focused air-path sheet and a focused condensate sheet, moving the indicator to FIG. 6, so no part was deleted and no sheet carries more than eight numerals. Cancelled two claims and renumbered to 21, restored the brief's working title, and made the gasket name and the sectional-view designations consistent.
reasoning: Every deletion was made by removing the drafter's invention rather than by rewriting the invention. Where a sentence carried both supported and unsupported content, only the unsupported part came out: the cassette sentence keeps the opposed, mutually facing arrangement across the central space and drops the sealed rigid container; the retention paragraph keeps compression of the resilient feet between the ledges and the load path from the lid and drops the tolerance-stack rationale; the circulation paragraph keeps the separation of the supply and return legs by the tray side walls and drops the mixing and sweeping results.

Two claims were cancelled rather than narrowed, because their whole subject matter was untraced: the perforation location and distribution claim, and the conductive-contact claim. Claim 6 was amended down to cassette removability, which the disclosure supports through fitting conditioned cassettes to the spacer frame. Renumbering produced 21 claims whose dependencies point only at claims 1, 3, 7, 10, 14 and 18, and I verified that each antecedent precedes its dependents.

The perforation contradiction was resolved in favour of the flow that claim 1, the method claim, the abstract and the inventor sentence all describe: the descending stream passes through the perforations and returns through the lower return passage, from which it rises through the product region. The sentence that had the perforations feeding the product region along the tray length was the one that was also unsupported, so a single deletion cured both findings.

The peripheral outlet openings and the discharge openings were both recited at the lower ends of the guide ducts with nothing separating them. Adding 'separate from the peripheral outlet openings' in claims 8 and 17, in the description and in the summary distinguishes them in words, and the drawings now distinguish them in place: the outlet opens sideways through the outboard face of the duct into the side supply passage (FIG. 4), while the discharge opening passes through the downwardly facing bottom surface (FIG. 5).

Adding the peripheral outlet opening to the former lower-side sheet would have made nine numerals on one sheet. Rather than drop a disclosed part or a numeral definition, that sheet was split into FIG. 4 (air path: tray side wall, side supply passage, perforations, guide duct, peripheral outlet opening) and FIG. 5 (condensate path: guide duct, discharge opening, condensate channel, absorbent wick, pull tab), with the indicator moved to FIG. 6. All 31 numerals still appear on at least one sheet, no sheet exceeds eight, and every brief stays under the character ceiling.

Figure briefs were shortened by removing invented rendering substance, not by weakening the geometry: the frame proportions in all three axes, the count and corner placement of the resilient feet, the integral formation of the rib, the stepped bore, shoulder and collar, and the equal wall heights and lower-two-thirds placement in FIG. 1 are gone. Bodies whose appearance the source does not give are now identified as shown schematically, which keeps the depiction a convention rather than an embodiment. Where a body appears only as context, it is described generically so no sheet names a part it does not list.

The drawing formalities were cured without adding technical matter: FIG. 1 is designated a schematic vertical sectional view, FIGS. 3, 4 and 5 are enlarged views of identified regions of FIG. 1, and FIG. 6 is an enlarged schematic sectional view through a wall of the shell. No figure now claims to be taken on a cutting plane, so no section line or repeated designation is required.

The title was returned to the working title in the drafting brief. The expanded wording would have needed the applicant's confirmation, and this draft cannot ask a question, so the brief, which is the authority for filing formalities, governs.
