Every finding has been fixed and the files are back in step.

Untraced technical matter is gone. The shell and lid are now simply formed of thermally insulating material; the tray-foot, resilient-foot and wick alternatives are deleted; a cassette now holds a phase-change material with no statement about how it is built; the cassettes-clear-of-the-tray relationship and its no-contact effect are deleted and claim 6 is reduced to cassette removability; the perforation wall, hole shapes and lengthwise distribution are deleted and that dependent claim is cancelled; the indicator's bore, stepped shoulder, collar and latch recess are removed from the description and the drawing, leaving stem, latch and spring; conductive contact is back to thermally coupled in the description and the figure and that claim is cancelled; and the exposed-position variants, the rib and channel length variant, the outlet-form variant, the lower-return-passage thermal result and the tolerance-stack sentence are all removed.

The internal conflicts are resolved. The perforations open from the side supply passages into the lower return passage in every place they are described, which matches claim 1, the method claim, the abstract and the inventor's sentence. The discharge openings are now recited as separate from the peripheral outlet openings in the description, the summary and claims 8 and 17, and the drawings separate them physically: the air outlet passes sideways through the outboard face of the guide duct into the side supply passage, and the condensate opening passes through the duct's downwardly facing bottom surface. FIG. 1 shows the lid overlying the shell top ends with that interface enlarged in FIG. 3, FIG. 6 shows the cassette confronting the stem across the intervening space, and numeral 100 now carries a lead line with an arrow to the assembly as a whole.

Because adding the peripheral outlet opening would have put nine numerals on the lower side sheet, that sheet was split rather than trimmed of a disclosed part: FIG. 4 carries the air path and FIG. 5 the condensate path, and the indicator moved to FIG. 6. All 31 numerals appear on at least one sheet, no sheet carries more than eight, and every brief is under the character ceiling.

On formalities, FIG. 1 is designated schematic, FIGS. 3, 4 and 5 are enlarged views of identified regions of FIG. 1, and FIG. 6 is an enlarged schematic sectional view, so no figure asserts an undesignated cutting plane. The part is called the compressible lid gasket everywhere, including claim 19 and the drawing description. The title is restored to the working title given in the drafting brief. The claim set is renumbered to 21 claims, with dependencies referring only to claims 1, 3, 7, 10, 14 and 18.

Removed all untraced technical matter (material menus, cassette construction, non-contact cooling, perforation placement and distribution, indicator internal mechanism, conductive contact, exposed-position variants, rib/channel and outlet-form variants, and two asserted performance results). Resolved the perforation flow contradiction, distinguished the discharge openings from the peripheral outlet openings, and harmonised the guide-duct air outlet, the lid-to-shell interface, the indicator geometry and the numeral 100 target across the drawings. reasoning: Every deletion was made by removing the drafter's invention rather than by rewriting the invention. Where a sentence carried both supported and unsupported content, only the unsupported part came out: the cassette sentence keeps the opposed, mutually facing arrangement across the central space and drops the sealed rigid container; the retention paragraph keeps compression of the resilient feet between the ledges and the load path from the lid and drops the tolerance-stack rationale; the circulation paragraph keeps the separation of the supply and return legs by the tray side walls and drops the mixing and sweeping results.

Two claims were cancelled rather than narrowed, because their whole subject matter was untraced: the perforation location and distribution claim, and the conductive-contact claim. Claim 6 was amended down to cassette removability, which the disclosure supports through fitting conditioned cassettes to the spacer frame. Renumbering produced 21 claims whose dependencies point only at claims 1, 3, 7, 10, 14 and 18, and I verified that each antecedent precedes its dependents.

The perforation contradiction was resolved in favour of the flow that claim 1, the method claim, the abstract and the inventor sentence all describe: the descending stream passes through the perforations and returns through the lower return passage, from which it rises through the product region. The sentence that had the perforations feeding the product region along the tray length was the one that was also unsupported, so a single deletion cured both findings.

The peripheral outlet openings and the discharge openings were both recited at the lower ends of the guide ducts with nothing separating them. Adding 'separate from the peripheral outlet openings' in claims 8 and 17, in the description and in the summary distinguishes them in words, and the drawings now distinguish them in place: the outlet opens sideways through the outboard face of the duct into the side supply passage (FIG. 4), while the discharge opening passes through the downwardly facing bottom surface (FIG. 5).

Adding the peripheral outlet opening to the former lower-side sheet would have made nine numerals on one sheet. Rather than drop a disclosed part or a numeral definition, that sheet was split into FIG. 4 (air path: tray side wall, side supply passage, perforations, guide duct, peripheral outlet opening) and FIG. 5 (condensate path: guide duct, discharge opening, condensate channel, absorbent wick, pull tab), with the indicator moved to FIG. 6. All 31 numerals still appear on at least one sheet, no sheet exceeds eight, and every brief stays under the character ceiling.

Figure briefs were shortened by removing invented rendering substance, not by weakening the geometry: the frame proportions in all three axes, the count and corner placement of the resilient feet, the integral formation of the rib, the stepped bore, shoulder and collar, and the equal wall heights and lower-two-thirds placement in FIG. 1 are gone. Bodies whose appearance the source does not give are now identified as shown schematically, which keeps the depiction a convention rather than an embodiment. Where a body appears only as context, it is described generically so no sheet names a part it does not list.

The drawing formalities were cured without adding technical matter: FIG. 1 is designated a schematic vertical sectional view, FIGS. 3, 4 and 5 are enlarged views of identified regions of FIG. 1, and FIG. 6 is an enlarged schematic sectional view through a wall of the shell. No figure now claims to be taken on a cutting plane, so no section line or repeated designation is required.

The title was returned to the working title in the drafting brief. The expanded wording would have needed the applicant's confirmation, and this draft cannot ask a question, so the brief, which is the authority for filing formalities, governs.

FIG. 1 briefs the tray walls as continuous and the floor top surface as plain and flat where the feet stand, which is affirmatively inconsistent with a perforated tray side wall (FIG. 4) and with a trough sunk in the floor top surface at the foot of the side gap (FIG. 5).   - Suggested fix: Add to figures/fig-01.md, in Geometry to draw: "A narrow rib projects downward from the underside of the slab on each side, inboard of the top ends of the wall bodies, and a small compressible body lies between the slab underside and each top end. FIG. 6 is briefed with the stem in the exposed position and the spring "shown compressed", which depicts the spring as still storing the energy it is said to have already released. The figure therefore contradicts the recited operation of the same numbered parts 82 and 86.
  - Suggested fix: In figures/fig-06.md replace "drawn as aligned loops and shown compressed" with "drawn as aligned loops and shown extended, its loops spaced apart".

# FIG. 2

## View
Perspective view of the thermal module alone, seen from above and in front so that the open top, the near long side and the near short end are visible. Plain black line work on white, no hatching. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

## Geometry to draw
The main body is a rectangular open frame, shown schematically. It has a near long side wall, a far long side wall, a left short end wall, a right short end wall and a bottom panel joining them. The top is open. This frame is the spacer frame 42; the spacer frame 42 together with the two slabs it holds is the thermal module 40.

Two flat rectangular slabs stand upright inside the frame, each parallel to the long side walls and running most of the frame length. They are spaced apart across the depth of the frame, leaving an open central gap between their confronting broad faces, and each is also spaced from the adjacent long side wall, leaving an open vertical channel between slab and wall. The slab nearer the front is the first phase-change cassette 44; the slab nearer the back is the second phase-change cassette 46. Each slab is a plain closed box, shown schematically.

In the bottom panel, within the open central gap between the slabs, a rectangular through opening is drawn, so the viewer looks down through the panel there. This opening is the central inlet opening 48.

Along the lower part of the near long side wall, at the foot of the channel between the first phase-change cassette 44 and that wall, a single rectangular opening passes through the wall. This is one of the peripheral outlet openings 54. A matching opening is drawn in the far long side wall where visible.

The top edge of the near long side wall carries an upwardly open groove at mid-length, running across the thickness of that wall. This groove is the mating channel 56.

Small blocks project downward from the underside of the frame, two visible at the front, shown schematically. These blocks are the resilient feet 58.

## Reference numerals on this sheet
40, 42, 44, 46, 48, 54, 56, 58

- 40: outside the frame outline, clear of all line work, with a lead line and arrow directed at the module as a whole.

- 54: on the opening in the near long side wall.

In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.

The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12.

The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. The tray side walls 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.

The thermal module

Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by a given payload are fitted before packing and exchanged between shipments.

The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, located beside the phase-change cassettes, each guide duct 50 lying outboard of an outer face of one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame 42, each peripheral outlet opening 54 being at a lower end of one of the guide ducts 50.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58 at lower outboard regions of the spacer frame 42. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 that extends around the underside of the insulated lid 60 outboard of the depending indexing rib 62. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is then created by closing the lid, which is an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

Each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Circulation is driven by the density difference between air warmed in the product region and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes. The geometry supports that difference rather than substituting for it: the cooled air is produced at the top of the carrier and is given a continuous downward path of its own along the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, while the warmed air is given a continuous upward path through the product region to the central inlet opening 48, and the two paths meet only at the central inlet opening 48 and beneath the product tray 20. Because the supply and return legs are separated by the tray side walls 26 rather than sharing one opening, the descending cooled stream is not obliged to pass through the ascending warmed stream.

A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70. Discharge openings 76, separate from the peripheral outlet openings 54, are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. Referring to FIG. 6, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44 when the thermal module 40 is in the registered position.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again and the temperature-responsive latch 84 has returned to its retaining condition, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.

In use, phase-change cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by the payload are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.

The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.

The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12.

The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. The tray side walls 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.

Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by a given payload are fitted before packing and exchanged between shipments.

The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, located beside the phase-change cassettes, each guide duct 50 lying beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54, each peripheral outlet opening 54 being at a lower end of one of the guide ducts 50.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 need only be dropped into the outer shell 10 approximately, and may be set down offset or skewed within the clearance available to it. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is then created by closing the lid, which is an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 project inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10 beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. The rising stream divides along the confronting inner faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams that travel outward over the cassette faces. Each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Circulation is driven by the density difference between air warmed in the product region and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.

Operation

In use, phase-change cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by the payload are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. Goods are placed in the product tray 20 and the product tray 20 is placed in the outer shell 10 so that the tray feet 22 stand on the floor 12, leaving the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20 and the two side supply passages 28 between the tray side walls 26 and the side walls 14. Alternatives

Two phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42, opposed across the central space. Entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.

The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12.

The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. The tray side walls 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.

The thermal module

Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by a given payload are fitted before packing and exchanged between shipments.

The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, located beside the phase-change cassettes, each guide duct 50 lying beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54, each peripheral outlet opening 54 being at a lower end of one of the guide ducts 50.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and the registration is completed by the closing of the lid. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is therefore created by an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 of the outer shell 10 lie beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. The resilient feet 58 maintain a downward holding force during transport, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.

The circulation path

In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the confronting inner faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams that travel outward over the cassette faces. Each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Circulation is driven by the density difference between air warmed in the product region and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes. The geometry supports that difference rather than substituting for it: the cooled air is produced at the top of the carrier and is given a continuous downward path of its own along the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, while the warmed air is given a continuous upward path through the product region to the central inlet opening 48, and the two paths meet only at the central inlet opening 48 and beneath the product tray 20. Because the supply and return legs are separated by the tray side walls 26 rather than sharing one opening, the descending cooled stream is not obliged to pass through the ascending warmed stream.

Condensate management

A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough that extends around the product tray 20 at a lower region of the outer shell 10, beneath the side supply passages 28. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70. Discharge openings 76, separate from the peripheral outlet openings 54, are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. Referring to FIG. 6, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44 when the thermal module 40 is in the registered position.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again and the temperature-responsive latch 84 has returned to its retaining condition, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.

In use, phase-change cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by the payload are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. Two phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42, opposed across the central space. Entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The described implementations are examples. A person skilled in the art may combine, substitute or omit the described features within the scope of the claims that follow.

In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.

The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12.

The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. The tray side walls 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.

The thermal module

Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by a given payload are fitted before packing and exchanged between shipments.

The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, located beside the phase-change cassettes, each guide duct 50 lying beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54, each peripheral outlet opening 54 being at a lower end of one of the guide ducts 50.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and the registration is completed by the closing of the lid. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is therefore created by an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 of the outer shell 10 lie beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. The resilient feet 58 maintain a downward holding force during transport, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.

The circulation path

In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Air warmed in the product region rises to the central inlet opening 48, and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes descends through the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, so that circulation proceeds without any powered air mover.

Condensate management

A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough that extends around the product tray 20 at a lower region of the outer shell 10, beneath the side supply passages 28. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70. Discharge openings 76, separate from the peripheral outlet openings 54, are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

Mechanical exposure indicator

The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. Referring to FIG. 6, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44 when the thermal module 40 is in the registered position.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again and the temperature-responsive latch 84 has returned to its retaining condition, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.

Operation

In use, phase-change cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by the payload are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. Goods are placed in the product tray 20 and the product tray 20 is placed in the outer shell 10 so that the tray feet 22 stand on the floor 12, leaving the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20 and the two side supply passages 28 between the tray side walls 26 and the side walls 14. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20. The insulated lid 60 is then closed, whereby the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 and shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position, the resilient feet 58 are pressed against the ledges 18 to retain the thermal module 40, and the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. Air thereafter circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover. At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.

Alternatives

Two phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42, opposed across the central space. Entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.

The described implementations are examples. A person skilled in the art may combine, substitute or omit the described features within the scope of the claims that follow.

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and the registration is completed by the closing of the lid. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is therefore created by an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 of the outer shell 10 lie beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. The resilient feet 58 maintain a downward holding force during transport, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.

The circulation path

In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Air warmed in the product region rises to the central inlet opening 48, and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes descends through the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, so that circulation proceeds without any powered air mover.

Condensate management

A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough that extends around the product tray 20. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70. Discharge openings 76 at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

Mechanical exposure indicator

The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. Referring to FIG. 6, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again and the temperature-responsive latch 84 has returned to its retaining condition, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.

Operation

In use, phase-change cassettes conditioned to the temperature required by the payload are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. Goods are placed in the product tray 20 and the product tray 20 is placed in the outer shell 10 so that the tray feet 22 stand on the floor 12, leaving the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20 and the two side supply passages 28 between the tray side walls 26 and the side walls 14. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20. The insulated lid 60 is then closed, whereby the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 and shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position, the resilient feet 58 are pressed against the ledges 18 to retain the thermal module 40, and the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. Air thereafter circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover. At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.

Alternatives

Two phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42, opposed across the central space. Entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.

The described implementations are examples. A person skilled in the art may combine, substitute or omit the described features within the scope of the claims that follow.

A passive cold-chain carrier is disclosed in which the closing of the lid, rather than the care of the packer, establishes the circulation path.

In one aspect, the carrier includes an insulated outer shell having a floor and side walls, a product tray removably received in the outer shell, a thermal module removably received in the outer shell above the product tray, and an insulated lid. The product tray is supported above the floor by tray feet so that a lower return passage remains between the product tray and the floor, and the tray side walls are spaced inward from the side walls of the outer shell to form two side supply passages. The thermal module includes a rigid spacer frame and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame, the spacer frame defining a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings. The insulated lid carries a depending indexing rib positioned to enter a mating channel of the spacer frame as the lid closes and to shift the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages.

In the registered position the shell, the product tray, the thermal module and the lid cooperate to define a circulation path along which air rising from a product region within the product tray enters the central inlet opening, divides along faces of the two phase-change cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage. The carrier is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover, and the circulation is driven by the density difference between the air warmed in the product region and the air cooled along the cassette faces.

The technical effect of lid-driven registration is that the alignment on which the circulation path depends is created by an act the packer cannot omit. The thermal module may be dropped into the outer shell approximately, offset or skewed, and the depending indexing rib entering the mating channel translates the module into the position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages. The seal made by a compressible lid gasket against the upper edge of the outer shell occurs after registration, so the carrier is not closed against a module that is still out of position. The same closing movement presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the outer shell, so that the registered module is held down against the product tray and cannot lift away from it under the vibration and inversion of transport.

In a further aspect, a shallow condensate channel extends around the product tray and receives a removable absorbent wick. Discharge openings at lower ends of the guide ducts, separate from the peripheral outlet openings, deliver condensate into the condensate channel. A pull tab on the absorbent wick remains accessible when the product tray is removed, so the wick is replaced without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service.

In a further aspect, the outer shell carries a mechanical exposure indicator visible from outside the carrier. An indicator stem is thermally coupled to one of the phase-change cassettes and is retained by a temperature-responsive latch. If that cassette softens enough to release the latch, a spring moves the indicator stem to a latched exposed position, and the indication remains exposed after the cassette cools again, being reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The indicator therefore reports the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends, survives recovery of the cassette, and requires no battery. The exposure indicator does not control airflow, so the circulation path is unaffected by whether the indicator has tripped.

In a further aspect, a method includes fitting conditioned phase-change cassettes to the spacer frame, placing product in the product tray, placing the product tray in the outer shell, placing the thermal module above the product tray, and closing the insulated lid so that the depending indexing rib enters the mating channel and shifts the thermal module into the registered position, whereafter air circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover.

The features summarised above may be used together or separately, and the summary is not a statement of the scope of the claims.

1. A passive cold-chain carrier comprising:

an insulated outer shell having a floor, side walls and an upper edge;

a product tray removably received in the outer shell, the product tray having a bottom wall, tray side walls, perforations, and tray feet standing on the floor so that the product tray is supported above the floor and a lower return passage remains between the bottom wall and the floor, the tray side walls being spaced inward from the side walls of the outer shell so that two side supply passages are formed;

a thermal module removably received in the outer shell above the product tray, the thermal module comprising a rigid spacer frame and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame, the spacer frame defining a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts located beside the phase-change cassettes, peripheral outlet openings at lower ends of the guide ducts, and a mating channel; and

an insulated lid closable on the upper edge of the outer shell and carrying a depending indexing rib positioned to enter the mating channel as the insulated lid closes and to shift the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages;

the carrier being free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover, and the outer shell, the product tray, the thermal module and the insulated lid cooperating in the registered position to define a circulation path along which air rising from a product region within the product tray enters the central inlet opening, divides along faces of the two phase-change cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through the perforations, and returns through the lower return passage.

2. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the spacer frame carries resilient feet, the outer shell has ledges beneath the resilient feet, and closure of the insulated lid presses the resilient feet against the ledges so that the thermal module is held down against lifting away from the product tray.

3. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, further comprising a compressible lid gasket carried by the insulated lid and arranged to seal against the upper edge of the outer shell after the depending indexing rib has shifted the thermal module into the registered position.

4. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the two opposed phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame with an inner face of a first phase-change cassette confronting an inner face of a second phase-change cassette across a central space, and the central inlet opening opens downward into the central space.

5. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame.

6. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, further comprising a shallow condensate channel extending around the product tray, and a removable absorbent wick lying in the condensate channel.

7. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 6, wherein openings at lower ends of the guide ducts discharge condensate into the condensate channel.

8. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 6, wherein the absorbent wick carries a pull tab that remains accessible when the product tray is removed from the outer shell, so that the absorbent wick is replaceable without opening a phase-change cassette.

9. # FIG. 1

## View
Schematic vertical sectional view of an assembled passive cold-chain carrier. Plain black line work on white, section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area.

## Geometry to draw
Two thick hatched upright wall bodies, joined at the bottom by a thick hatched horizontal bottom body, form an upright container at the centre of the drawing area, open at the top. These are the sectioned outer shell 10, whose bottom body is the floor 12. A block projects inward from each wall body below its top end.

A thick hatched horizontal slab lies across the top ends of both wall bodies, overlying those top ends. This slab is the insulated lid 60, closed. A narrow rib projects downward from its underside on each side, inboard of those top ends, and a small compressible body lies between the slab and each top end. That interface is enlarged in FIG. 3.

Inside the container, a sectioned open-top box with thin hatched upright walls and a horizontal bottom wall is the product tray 20. Its bottom wall is raised above the floor 12, and its outer side surfaces stand clear of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap on each side running down to the floor 12. Below the level of that bottom wall, small openings pass through each upright wall of the box.

Two short hatched blocks stand between the tray bottom wall and the floor 12. These blocks are the tray feet 22. The open space between the tray bottom wall and the floor 12 is the lower return passage 24. A shallow upwardly open trough is formed in the floor 12 at the foot of each vertical gap, with an elongated absorbent body lying in it.

Between the open top of the product tray 20 and the underside of the insulated lid 60, an elongated hatched body is drawn in section. This body is the thermal module 40. Two upright plain rectangular blocks are drawn within it, shown schematically, spaced from one another and from its ends. The body is open downward at its centre, and an open vertical channel runs down through it outboard of each block, opening through its outboard side above the vertical gap.

## Reference numerals on this sheet
10, 12, 20, 22, 24, 40, 60, 100

## Numeral targets
- 10: well inside the hatching of the left wall body.
- 12: well inside the hatching of the bottom body.
- 20: well inside the left upright wall of the open-top box.
- 22: well inside the left short block on the floor.
- 24: inside the open space between the tray bottom wall and the floor.
- 40: outside the container, clear of all line work, with a lead line and arrow directed at the module as a whole.
- 60: well inside the horizontal slab at the top.
- 100: outside the container, clear of all line work, with a lead line and arrow directed at the assembled carrier as a whole.

Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, located beside the phase-change cassettes, each guide duct 50 lying beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54, each peripheral outlet opening 54 being at a lower end of one of the guide ducts 50.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and the registration is completed by the closing of the lid. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is therefore created by an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 of the outer shell 10 lie beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. The resilient feet 58 maintain a downward holding force during transport, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.

Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.

The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.
