# FIG. 5

## View
Enlarged view of the condensate channel region of FIG. 1, seen horizontally in section. Plain black line work on white, diagonal section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

## Geometry to draw
A thick hatched upright insulating wall body occupies the left portion of the drawing area, running from the upper part of the fragment down to a thick hatched horizontal bottom body that occupies the lower part and extends rightward.

In the upper right part of the drawing area, a hatched body fragment is drawn in section. An open vertical channel passes down through this fragment, bounded by hatched material to its left and right. This channel is one of the guide ducts 50. At the lower end of the channel, an opening passes through the downwardly facing bottom surface of the fragment. This opening is one of the discharge openings 76.

Below the body fragment, a thin hatched upright wall is drawn in section, spaced to the right of the inner surface of the upright wall body and meeting the upwardly facing top surface of the horizontal bottom body just inboard of the trough described below. An open vertical space runs down between the upright wall body and the thin wall, from beneath the body fragment to the horizontal bottom body, so that the downward opening in the fragment stands above that space.

In the upwardly facing top surface of the horizontal bottom body, at the foot of the open vertical space and below the discharge opening 76, a shallow upwardly open trough is drawn in section, wider than it is deep. This trough is the condensate channel 70.

An elongated body of absorbent material lies in the trough, filling its lower part, shown schematically. This body is the absorbent wick 72. A narrow strip extends upward from its upper surface into the open vertical space, its free upper end clear of the surrounding surfaces. This strip is the pull tab 74.

## Reference numerals on this sheet
50, 70, 72, 74, 76

- 50: inside the open vertical channel in the body fragment.
- 70: inside the trough at its left end, above the absorbent body.
- 72: well inside the elongated absorbent body lying in the trough.
- 74: well inside the narrow strip rising from the absorbent body.
- 76: on the opening through the bottom surface of the body fragment.

# FIG. 6

## View
Enlarged schematic sectional view, through a wall of the outer shell, of the mechanical exposure indicator, seen horizontally with the indicator stem in the exposed position. Plain black line work on white, section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

## Geometry to draw
A thick hatched upright wall body stands across the middle of the drawing area, its outer surface facing left and its inner surface facing right. This wall body is one of the side walls 14 of the sectioned outer shell 10.

Carried by the wall body, and drawn as a horizontally elongated plain rectangular outline extending through the thickness of the wall body from its outer surface to its inner surface, is the body of the mechanical exposure indicator 80, shown schematically and open at both of its ends.

An elongated horizontal shaft lies within that outline and extends beyond both of its ends: to the left the shaft projects past the outer surface of the wall body, and to the right its inner end reaches into the open space at the right of the drawing area. This shaft is the indicator stem 82.

A coil spring surrounds the shaft within the outline, drawn as aligned loops and shown extended, its loops spaced apart. This spring is the spring 86.

A small block sits above the shaft within the outline, to the right of the coil spring, projecting downward with its lower end adjacent the upper surface of the shaft, shown schematically. This block is the temperature-responsive latch 84.

In the open space at the right of the drawing area, an upright plain rectangular block is drawn, shown schematically, its left face spaced from and thermally coupled to the inner end of the shaft. This block is the first phase-change cassette 44. The spacer frame wall, the guide duct and the side supply passage that lie between the wall body and the cassette in the assembled carrier are omitted from this schematic detail view.

## Reference numerals on this sheet
10, 14, 44, 80, 82, 84, 86

## Numeral targets
- 10: outside the wall body, clear of line work, with a lead line and arrow to the outer shell as a whole.
- 14: well inside the hatching of the upright wall body, below the indicator outline.
- 44: well inside the upright rectangular block at the right.
- 80: on the outline of the indicator body carried by the wall body, at its left part clear of the shaft.
- 82: on the part of the shaft projecting left beyond the outer surface of the wall body.
- 84: well inside the small block above the shaft.
- 86: on one loop of the coil spring surrounding the shaft.

1. A passive cold-chain carrier comprising:

an insulated outer shell having a floor, side walls and an upper edge;

a product tray removably received in the outer shell, the product tray having a bottom wall, tray side walls, perforations, and tray feet standing on the floor so that the product tray is supported above the floor and a lower return passage remains between the bottom wall and the floor, the tray side walls being spaced inward from the side walls of the outer shell so that two side supply passages are formed;

a thermal module removably received in the outer shell above the product tray, the thermal module comprising a rigid spacer frame and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame, the spacer frame defining a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts located beside the phase-change cassettes, peripheral outlet openings at lower ends of the guide ducts, and a mating channel; and

an insulated lid closable on the upper edge of the outer shell and carrying a depending indexing rib positioned to enter the mating channel as the insulated lid closes and to shift the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages;

the carrier being free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover, and the outer shell, the product tray, the thermal module and the insulated lid cooperating in the registered position to define a circulation path along which air rising from a product region within the product tray enters the central inlet opening, divides along faces of the two phase-change cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through the perforations, and returns through the lower return passage.

2. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the spacer frame carries resilient feet, the outer shell has ledges beneath the resilient feet, and closure of the insulated lid presses the resilient feet against the ledges so that the thermal module is held down against lifting away from the product tray.

3. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, further comprising a compressible lid gasket carried by the insulated lid and arranged to seal against the upper edge of the outer shell after the depending indexing rib has shifted the thermal module into the registered position.

4. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the two opposed phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame with an inner face of a first phase-change cassette confronting an inner face of a second phase-change cassette across a central space, and the central inlet opening opens downward into the central space.

5. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame.

6. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, further comprising a shallow condensate channel extending around the product tray, and a removable absorbent wick lying in the condensate channel.

7. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 6, wherein the spacer frame further defines discharge openings, separate from the peripheral outlet openings, at lower ends of the guide ducts, the discharge openings discharging condensate into the condensate channel.

8. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 6, wherein the absorbent wick carries a pull tab that remains accessible when the product tray is removed from the outer shell, so that the absorbent wick is replaceable without opening a phase-change cassette.

9. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, further comprising a mechanical exposure indicator carried by the outer shell and visible from outside the carrier, the mechanical exposure indicator comprising an indicator stem thermally coupled to one of the phase-change cassettes, a temperature-responsive latch retaining the indicator stem in a stowed position, and a spring biasing the indicator stem toward an exposed position, the temperature-responsive latch releasing the indicator stem when said one of the phase-change cassettes softens.

10. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 9, wherein the exposed position is a latched position in which the mechanical exposure indicator retains the indicator stem after said one of the phase-change cassettes has cooled again, the mechanical exposure indicator being resettable manually only after the carrier is opened.

11. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 9, wherein the mechanical exposure indicator does not control airflow, the circulation path being the same whether or not the indicator stem stands in the exposed position.

12. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the depending indexing rib meets the mating channel while the insulated lid is spaced above the upper edge of the outer shell, and remaining closing travel of the insulated lid translates the spacer frame horizontally into the registered position.

13. A thermal module for a passive cold-chain carrier having an insulated outer shell, a product tray defining side supply passages with side walls of the outer shell, and an insulated lid carrying a depending indexing rib, the thermal module comprising:

a rigid spacer frame sized to be removably received in the outer shell above the product tray; and

two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame;

the spacer frame defining a central inlet opening through which air rising from a product region within the product tray enters the spacer frame, two downward guide ducts located beside the phase-change cassettes and receiving air that has divided along faces of the two phase-change cassettes, peripheral outlet openings at lower ends of the guide ducts, and a mating channel positioned to be entered by the depending indexing rib as the insulated lid closes so that the thermal module is shifted into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages.

14. The thermal module of claim 13, further comprising resilient feet carried by the spacer frame, the resilient feet being positioned to be pressed against ledges of the outer shell by closure of the insulated lid so that the thermal module is held down against the product tray.

15. The thermal module of claim 13, wherein the mating channel opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame.

16. The thermal module of claim 13, wherein the spacer frame further defines discharge openings, separate from the peripheral outlet openings, at the lower ends of the guide ducts and positioned to discharge condensate into a condensate channel of the outer shell.

17. A method of transporting temperature-sensitive goods, the method comprising:

fitting two conditioned phase-change cassettes to a rigid spacer frame of a thermal module, the spacer frame defining a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts located beside the phase-change cassettes, peripheral outlet openings at lower ends of the guide ducts, and a mating channel;

placing the goods in a product tray and placing the product tray in an insulated outer shell so that tray feet of the product tray stand on a floor of the outer shell, leaving a lower return passage between the product tray and the floor and two side supply passages between tray side walls of the product tray and side walls of the outer shell;

placing the thermal module in the outer shell above the product tray;

closing an insulated lid on an upper edge of the outer shell so that a depending indexing rib carried by the insulated lid enters the mating channel and shifts the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages; and

thereafter transporting the goods while air circulates, without operation of any powered air mover, along a circulation path in which air rising from a product region within the product tray enters the central inlet opening, divides along faces of the two phase-change cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage.

18. The method of claim 17, wherein closing the insulated lid further presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the outer shell, retaining the thermal module against lifting away from the product tray during the transporting, and compresses a compressible lid gasket against the upper edge of the outer shell after the thermal module has been shifted into the registered position.

19. The method of claim 17, further comprising, after the transporting, opening the insulated lid, removing the product tray from the outer shell, and drawing a removable absorbent wick out of a condensate channel of the outer shell by a pull tab of the absorbent wick without opening a phase-change cassette.

20. The method of claim 17, further comprising reading, from outside the outer shell, a mechanical exposure indicator having an indicator stem thermally coupled to one of the phase-change cassettes, the indicator stem having been moved by a spring to a latched exposed position on release of a temperature-responsive latch by softening of said one of the phase-change cassettes and remaining in the latched exposed position after said one of the phase-change cassettes has cooled again, and resetting the mechanical exposure indicator manually after the insulated lid has been opened.

In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.

The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12.

The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. The tray side walls 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.

The thermal module

Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 before packing.

The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, each guide duct 50 located beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54, each peripheral outlet opening 54 being at a lower end of one of the guide ducts 50.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and the registration is completed by the closing of the lid. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is therefore created by an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 of the outer shell 10 lie beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. The resilient feet 58 maintain a downward holding force during transport, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.

The circulation path

In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Air warmed in the product region rises to the central inlet opening 48, and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes descends through the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, so that circulation proceeds without any powered air mover.

Condensate management

A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough formed in the outer shell 10 and extending around the product tray 20. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the condensate channel 70 and the absorbent wick 72 remain in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed. Discharge openings 76, separate from the peripheral outlet openings 54, are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

Mechanical exposure indicator

The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. Referring to FIG. 6, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.

The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.

The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12.

The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. The tray side walls 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.

The thermal module

Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 before packing.

The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, each guide duct 50 located beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 aligned with the side supply passages 28.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and the registration is completed by the closing of the lid. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is therefore created by an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 of the outer shell 10 lie beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. The resilient feet 58 maintain a downward holding force during transport, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.

In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Air warmed in the product region rises to the central inlet opening 48, and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes descends through the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, so that circulation proceeds without any powered air mover.

A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough formed in the outer shell 10 and extending around the product tray 20. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the condensate channel 70 and the absorbent wick 72 remain in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed. Discharge openings 76, separate from the peripheral outlet openings 54, are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. Alternatives

# FIG. 1

## View
Schematic vertical sectional view of an assembled passive cold-chain carrier. Plain black line work on white, section hatching on cut material, all line work inside the drawing area.

## Geometry to draw
Two thick hatched upright wall bodies joined at the bottom by a thick hatched horizontal bottom body form an upright container, open at the top. These are the sectioned outer shell 10, its bottom body being the floor 12. A block projects inward from each wall body below its top end.

A thick hatched horizontal slab across the top ends of both wall bodies is the insulated lid 60, closed. A narrow rib projects downward from its underside inboard of the left wall body top end, and a small compressible body lies between the slab and each top end.

Inside the container, a sectioned open-top box with thin hatched upright walls and a bottom wall is the product tray 20. Its bottom wall is raised above the floor 12 and its outer side surfaces stand clear of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap on each side. Small openings pass through each upright wall below the bottom wall level, and each upright wall stops short of the floor 12.

Two short hatched blocks between the tray bottom wall and the floor 12 are the tray feet 22. The open space between that bottom wall and the floor 12 is the lower return passage 24. A shallow upwardly open trough in the floor 12 at each gap foot holds an elongated absorbent body.

Between the open top of the product tray 20 and the lid 60, an elongated hatched body drawn in section is the thermal module 40. Two upright plain rectangular blocks, shown schematically, stand within it, spaced from one another and from its ends. The body is open downward at its centre, and an open vertical channel runs down through it outboard of each block, opening through its outboard side above the gap. An upwardly open groove in its top surface receives the lower end of the narrow rib.

Three thin broken-line closed curves enclose the upper left region with the rib, groove and left wall top; the lower left region with the outboard channel opening, the left gap and the tray openings; and the region with the trough and absorbent body. They indicate the regions enlarged in FIGS. 3, 4 and 5 respectively.

## Reference numerals on this sheet
10, 12, 20, 22, 24, 40, 60, 100

- 10: outside the container, with a lead line and arrow to the outer shell as a whole.
- 12: well inside the bottom body.

content.text:
All eight findings are fixed.

**Source fidelity at the duct outlets.** The phrase making the discharge openings a separate set is gone from claims 7 and 16 and from the Condensate management paragraph. The peripheral outlet openings are now recited only as aligned with the side supply passages in claims 1, 13 and 17 and in the description, while the duct-end location is kept only for the condensate discharge openings, which is where the disclosure puts it. FIG. 4 now says the opening lies where the channel meets the open vertical space, and the Brief Description of FIG. 4 matches.

**Figure briefs asserting undisclosed structure.** FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 no longer land the tray side wall on the floor: each upright wall stops short of the floor, and the exclusivity statement about the only communication path is deleted, so the tray remains supported on its feet and the return loop stays open. FIG. 6 now says only that structure lying between the wall body and the cassette in the assembled carrier is omitted from the schematic detail.

**Minor items.** FIG. 4 states that the fragment is taken between the ledges of the outer shell, so no ledge appears there and it no longer conflicts with FIG. 3. FIG. 6 shows the cassette face adjacent the inner end of the stem. FIG. 1 gains three broken-line curves enclosing the regions enlarged in FIGS. 3, 4 and 5, and the Brief Description entries for FIG. 1 and for each enlargement now refer to those broken lines. The section heading is now "Essential and optional features."

All six briefs are under the character ceiling, no sheet carries more than eight numerals, the numeral table is unchanged, and the claim set remains 20 claims depending only on claims 1, 6, 9, 13 and 17.

input.summary: Fixed all eight findings. Deleted the separateness of the discharge openings from claims 7 and 16 and the description; recited the peripheral outlet openings only as aligned with the side supply passages in claims 1, 13 and 17 and the description, leaving the duct-end location to the condensate openings; lifted the tray side wall off the floor in FIGS. 1 and 5 and removed the exclusive-path statement; reduced the FIG. 6 omission note to a neutral statement and made the cassette face adjacent the stem; added a note to FIG. 4 that the fragment is taken between the ledges; added broken-line region indications to FIG. 1 with matching Brief Description entries; and renamed the Alternatives heading to Essential and optional features.
reasoning: The critical item was cured by deletion in all three places at once, so the claims and description now say the same thing: the spacer frame defines discharge openings at lower ends of the guide ducts that discharge condensate, with no assertion that they are a second set of apertures. Numerals 54 and 76 remain distinct definitions in the table, and each is still drawn at the position its own figure sentence gives, but no text asserts a structural distinction the source does not make.

For the peripheral outlet openings I moved the only source-given attribute into the claims: alignment with the side supply passages. That attribute is what the registration limitation acts on, so claim 1 loses nothing operative by dropping the duct-end position, and the overlap-in-the-registered-position language that carries the invention is untouched in claims 1, 13 and 17. The duct-end wording now appears only where the disclosure uses it, for the condensate openings in claims 7 and 16.

The FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 skirt contact was an undisclosed contact and an exclusivity claim, and it also closed the loop the description depends on. Both briefs now have the tray wall stop short of the floor, which keeps the tray supported on its feet as the disclosure states and leaves the returning air a drawn path back to the product region. The perforations remain drawn below the tray bottom wall in FIG. 4, so the described route through them is still depicted without the figure asserting it is the only route.

This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.

A reusable passive cold-chain carrier has an insulated outer shell, a removable product tray, a removable thermal module, and an insulated lid. The product tray is suspended above the shell floor by feet so that a lower return passage remains under the tray. The tray side walls are spaced inward from the shell side walls to form two side supply passages.

The thermal module is a rigid spacer frame holding two opposed phase-change cassettes. The spacer frame rests above the product tray and below the lid. It includes a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings aligned with the side supply passages. Warm air rising from the product region enters the central inlet, divides along faces of the cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage. The carrier is passive. It has no fan, pump, or powered air mover.

The lid carries a depending indexing rib. As the lid closes, the rib enters a mating channel in the spacer frame and shifts the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages. A compressible lid gasket seals against the upper edge of the shell after registration. The same closing movement presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the shell so that the module cannot lift away from the tray during transport.

A removable absorbent wick lies in a shallow condensate channel around the product tray. Openings at the lower ends of the guide ducts discharge condensate into the channel. A pull tab on the wick remains accessible when the product tray is removed, allowing the wick to be replaced without opening a phase-change cassette.

The shell includes a mechanical exposure indicator visible from outside. An indicator stem is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette and retained by a temperature-responsive latch. If that cassette softens enough to release the latch, a spring moves the indicator stem to a latched exposed position. The indication remains exposed after the cassette cools again and is reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The indicator does not control airflow.

For use, conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame, products are placed in the tray, the thermal module is placed above the tray, and the lid is closed to register and retain the module. The disclosed essential relationship is the registered passive circulation path around the removable tray and opposed cassettes, combined with lid-driven registration of the thermal module. The wick and the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator are supported optional features.

A reusable passive cold-chain carrier has an insulated outer shell, a removable product tray, a removable thermal module, and an insulated lid. The product tray is suspended above the shell floor by feet so that a lower return passage remains under the tray. The tray side walls are spaced inward from the shell side walls to form two side supply passages.

The thermal module is a rigid spacer frame holding two opposed phase-change cassettes. The spacer frame rests above the product tray and below the lid. It includes a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings aligned with the side supply passages. Warm air rising from the product region enters the central inlet, divides along faces of the cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage. The carrier is passive. It has no fan, pump, or powered air mover.

The lid carries a depending indexing rib. As the lid closes, the rib enters a mating channel in the spacer frame and shifts the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages. A compressible lid gasket seals against the upper edge of the shell after registration. The same closing movement presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the shell so that the module cannot lift away from the tray during transport.

A removable absorbent wick lies in a shallow condensate channel around the product tray. Openings at the lower ends of the guide ducts discharge condensate into the channel. A pull tab on the wick remains accessible when the product tray is removed, allowing the wick to be replaced without opening a phase-change cassette.

The shell includes a mechanical exposure indicator visible from outside. An indicator stem is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette and retained by a temperature-responsive latch. If that cassette softens enough to release the latch, a spring moves the indicator stem to a latched exposed position. The indication remains exposed after the cassette cools again and is reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The indicator does not control airflow.

For use, conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame, products are placed in the tray, the thermal module is placed above the tray, and the lid is closed to register and retain the module. The disclosed essential relationship is the registered passive circulation path around the removable tray and opposed cassettes, combined with lid-driven registration of the thermal module. The wick and the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator are supported optional features.

content.content:
1	Temperature-sensitive goods such as vaccines, biological samples, prepared meals and laboratory reagents are frequently shipped in insulated carriers that hold a payload within a target temperature band for a period of hours or days. Carriers of this general kind fall into two broad families. Powered carriers use a fan, a pump or another driven air mover, together with a power source, to force air over a cold source and through the payload space. Passive carriers omit the power source and rely on conduction from, and natural convection around, a refrigerant mass such as water ice, dry ice, gel packs or sealed cassettes charged with a phase-change material.
2	
3	Passive carriers are attractive because they have no battery to charge, no motor to fail and no electrical approval burden for air transport. They are also harder to control. When a refrigerant mass is simply laid on top of, beside or beneath a payload, the cooled air falls where gravity and the packing arrangement happen to send it. Items directly against the refrigerant are driven toward the cold end of the acceptable band or below it, while items on the far side of the payload sit in a stagnant warm layer. The result is a temperature spread across the payload that grows as the load is packed more densely, and that varies from shipment to shipment because it depends on how a particular packer arranged the goods and the refrigerant on a particular day.
4	
5	Attempts to impose a defined circulation path on a passive carrier run into a practical difficulty. The path is defined by clearances, by openings and by the alignment between them, and every one of those relationships is destroyed if the component that carries the openings is set down rotated, offset or skewed by a person working quickly at a packing bench. A carrier that circulates air well when it is assembled precisely, and poorly when it is not, delivers the variability it was intended to remove. Packing instructions, printed arrows and keyed corner blocks all depend on the packer looking, and none of them acts on a component that has already been set down out of position.
6	
7	Two further problems attend repeated reuse of a passive carrier. First, moist ambient air admitted each time the carrier is opened condenses on the cold surfaces of the refrigerant mass and runs down into the payload space, wetting labels and cartons and, over many cycles, leaving standing water in the base of the carrier. Where the refrigerant is a sealed cassette, drying the interior often means removing the cassette from service. Second, a passive carrier gives no account of itself. If the payload was exposed to a temperature excursion in transit, and the refrigerant has since recovered, an inspection at the receiving dock shows a cold carrier and a firm cassette, and the excursion leaves no trace. Electronic data loggers record such events but add cost, battery management and a reading step to every unit shipped, and they report a sensor location rather than the state of the refrigerant that the payload actually depends on.
8	
9	There remains a need for a reusable passive carrier that establishes the same circulation path around the payload every time it is closed, without a powered air mover and without relying on the care of the person who packed it, that manages the condensate produced by repeated opening without taking the refrigerant out of service, and that retains a visible mechanical record of a refrigerant temperature excursion after the refrigerant has recovered.
10

content.content:
1	In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.
2	
3	Overall arrangement
4	
5	Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.
6	
7	The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12.
8	
9	The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. The tray side walls 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.
10	
11	The thermal module
12	
13	Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 before packing.
14	
15	The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, each guide duct 50 located beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 aligned with the side supply passages 28.
16	
17	The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.
18	
19	Registration and retention by the lid
20	
21	The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.
22	
23	This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and the registration is completed by the closing of the lid. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is therefore created by an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.
24	
25	The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 of the outer shell 10 lie beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. The resilient feet 58 maintain a downward holding force during transport, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.
26	
27	The circulation path
28	
29	In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.
30	
31	The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Air warmed in the product region rises to the central inlet opening 48, and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes descends through the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, so that circulation proceeds without any powered air mover.
32	
33	Condensate management
34	
35	A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough formed in the outer shell 10 and extending around the product tray 20. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the condensate channel 70 and the absorbent wick 72 remain in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed. Discharge openings 76 are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.
36	
37	The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.
38	
39	Mechanical exposure indicator
40	
41	The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. Referring to FIG. 6, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44.
42	
43	The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.
44	
45	The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.
46	
47	The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.

The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12.

The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. The tray side walls 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.

The thermal module

Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 before packing.

The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, each guide duct 50 located beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 aligned with the side supply passages 28.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and the registration is completed by the closing of the lid. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is therefore created by an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 of the outer shell 10 lie beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. The resilient feet 58 maintain a downward holding force during transport, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.

The circulation path

In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Air warmed in the product region rises to the central inlet opening 48, and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes descends through the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, so that circulation proceeds without any powered air mover.

Condensate management

A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough formed in the outer shell 10 and extending around the product tray 20. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the condensate channel 70 and the absorbent wick 72 remain in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed. Discharge openings 76 are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

Mechanical exposure indicator

The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. Referring to FIG. 6, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.

Operation

In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. Goods are placed in the product tray 20 and the product tray 20 is placed in the outer shell 10 so that the tray feet 22 stand on the floor 12, leaving the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20 and the two side supply passages 28 between the tray side walls 26 and the side walls 14. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20. The insulated lid 60 is then closed, whereby the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 and shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position, the resilient feet 58 are pressed against the ledges 18 to retain the thermal module 40, and the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. Air thereafter circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover. At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.

Essential and optional features

Two phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42, opposed across the central space. Entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.

The described implementations are examples. A person skilled in the art may combine, substitute or omit the described features within the scope of the claims that follow.

# FIG. 1

Schematic vertical sectional view of an assembled passive cold-chain carrier. Plain black line work on white, section hatching on cut material, all line work inside the drawing area.

Two thick hatched upright wall bodies joined at the bottom by a thick hatched horizontal bottom body form an upright container, open at the top. These are the sectioned outer shell 10, its bottom body being the floor 12. A block projects inward from each wall body below its top end.

A thick hatched horizontal slab across the top ends of both wall bodies is the insulated lid 60, closed. A narrow rib projects downward from its underside inboard of the left wall body top end, and a small compressible body lies between the slab and each top end.

Inside the container, a sectioned open-top box with thin hatched upright walls and a bottom wall is the product tray 20. Its bottom wall is raised above the floor 12 and its outer side surfaces stand clear of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap on each side. Small openings pass through each upright wall below the bottom wall level, and each upright wall stops short of the floor 12.

Two short hatched blocks between the tray bottom wall and the floor 12 are the tray feet 22. The open space between that wall and the floor 12 is the lower return passage 24. A shallow upwardly open trough in the floor 12 at each gap foot holds an elongated absorbent body.

Between the open top of the product tray 20 and the lid 60, an elongated hatched body drawn in section is the thermal module 40. Two upright plain rectangular blocks, shown schematically, stand within it, spaced from one another and from its ends. The body is open downward at its centre, and an open vertical channel runs down through it outboard of each block, opening through its outboard side above the gap. An upwardly open groove in its top surface receives the lower end of the narrow rib.

Three thin broken-line closed curves enclose the upper left region with the rib, groove and left wall top; the lower left region with the outboard channel opening, the left gap and the tray openings; and the region with the trough and absorbent body. They indicate the regions enlarged in FIGS. 3, 4 and 5.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 10: outside the container, with a lead line and arrow to the outer shell as a whole.
- 12: well inside the bottom body.
- 20: well inside the left upright wall of the box.
- 22: inside the left short block.
- 24: inside the space beneath the tray bottom wall.
- 40: outside the container, with a lead line and arrow to the module as a whole.
- 60: well inside the slab at the top.
- 100: outside the container, with a lead line and arrow to the whole carrier.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged view of a lower side region of FIG. 1, seen horizontally in section. Plain black line work on white, section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

A thick hatched upright insulating wall body occupies the left portion of the drawing area and runs the full height of the fragment, its inner surface facing right. This fragment is taken at a position along that wall between the ledges of the outer shell, so no ledge appears in this view.

In the upper right part of the drawing area, a hatched body fragment is drawn in section. Its left face is spaced from the inner surface of the upright wall body, leaving an open vertical space between them. An open vertical channel passes down through this fragment, bounded by hatched material to its left and right. This channel is one of the guide ducts 50.

Where that channel meets the open vertical space, an opening passes through the left face of the body fragment, so that the channel opens sideways into that space between the fragment and the upright wall body. This opening is one of the peripheral outlet openings 54.

Below the body fragment, and spaced to the right of the inner surface of the upright wall body, a thin hatched upright wall is drawn in section and runs downward to the lower edge of the fragment. This thin wall is one of the tray side walls 26. The open vertical space continues down between the upright wall body and the thin wall, so that the space fed through the peripheral outlet opening 54 runs downward past the thin wall. This continuing space is one of the side supply passages 28.

A thin hatched horizontal bottom wall joins the thin upright wall and extends rightward, and the open space beneath that bottom wall is the lower return passage 24.

In the portion of the thin upright wall below that bottom wall, a series of small openings passes through it, so that the side supply passage 28 opens through them into the space beneath the bottom wall. These openings are the perforations 30.

- 26: well inside the hatching of the thin upright wall, above the small openings.
- 28: inside the open vertical space between the upright wall body and the thin wall.
- 30: on one of the small openings in the thin upright wall.
- 50: inside the open vertical channel in the body fragment.
- 54: on the opening through the left face of the body fragment.

# FIG. 2

Perspective view of the thermal module alone, seen from above and in front so that the open top, the near long side and the near short end are visible. Plain black line work on white, no hatching. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

The main body is a rectangular open frame, shown schematically. It has a near long side wall, a far long side wall, a left short end wall, a right short end wall and a bottom panel joining them. The top is open. This frame is the spacer frame 42; the spacer frame 42 together with the two slabs it holds is the thermal module 40.

Two flat rectangular slabs stand upright inside the frame, each parallel to the long side walls and running most of the frame length. They are spaced apart across the depth of the frame, leaving an open central gap between their confronting broad faces, and each is also spaced from the adjacent long side wall, leaving an open vertical channel between slab and wall. The slab nearer the front is the first phase-change cassette 44; the slab nearer the back is the second phase-change cassette 46. Each slab is a plain closed box, shown schematically.

In the bottom panel, within the open central gap between the slabs, a rectangular through opening is drawn, so the viewer looks down through the panel there. This opening is the central inlet opening 48.

Along the lower part of the near long side wall, at the foot of the channel between the first phase-change cassette 44 and that wall, a single rectangular opening passes through the wall. This is one of the peripheral outlet openings 54. A matching opening passes through the far long side wall at the corresponding position; it is hidden in this view and is not drawn.

The top edge of the near long side wall carries an upwardly open groove at mid-length, running across the thickness of that wall. This groove is the mating channel 56.

Small blocks project downward from the underside of the frame, two visible at the front, shown schematically. These blocks are the resilient feet 58.
