- 46: well inside the visible upper face of the rear slab.
- 48: well inside the through opening in the bottom panel.
- 54: on the opening in the near long side wall.
- 56: well inside the groove in the top edge of the near long side wall.
- 58: well inside one of the small blocks projecting below the frame at the front.

content.text:
The draft is now clean against both preflight failures. Summary of what I did:

**Review items fixed**
- `draft/07-drawings.md` and `figures/FIG-1.md` used the form "FIGS. 3, 4 and 5". The preflight parsed the trailing "4" and "5" as undefined reference numerals with no figure appearance. Both now read "FIG. 3, in FIG. 4 and in FIG. 5", so every digit in the specification is either a defined numeral or an explicit figure reference.
- `figures/FIG-4.md` carried the negative linework control "so no ledge appears in this view". It now states the required geometry positively: the wall body's inner surface is a flat vertical surface running straight from the top of the fragment to the bottom.

**Two small defects I corrected while in those files**
- `figures/FIG-5.md` had a run-on clause ("...upright wall body its lower edge stopping short of...") that made the spacing relationship ambiguous to a renderer; added the missing comma.
- `figures/FIG-2.md` and `figures/FIG-6.md` described hidden structure by saying it "is not drawn" / "is omitted". Both are now positive occlusion statements naming what is visible, so neither can be read as a generic linework ban.
- Claim 17 recited "peripheral outlet openings aligned with the side supply passages" in its first step, before the side supply passages were introduced in the second step. Removed the premature phrase; the registered-position step later in the same claim already ties the openings to the passages, so scope is unchanged and antecedent basis is clean.

Everything else in the body text I left alone.

input.summary: Cleared the two mechanical preflight failures and fixed three defects found while doing so. The bare "4" and "5" that the numeral checker complained about came from the phrase "FIGS. 3, 4 and 5" in the Brief Description of the Drawings and in the FIG. 1 brief; both now spell out each figure reference, so no digit in the specification is loose. The FIG. 4 brief's negative control "so no ledge appears in this view" is replaced by a positive statement of the wall's flat inner surface. I also repaired a run-on clause in the FIG. 5 brief, converted two "is not drawn" / "is omitted" statements in the FIG. 2 and FIG. 6 briefs into positive occlusion statements, and removed a premature reference to "the side supply passages" from the first step of method claim 17 where they had no antecedent. No body text, claim scope, disclosure content or numeral assignment was otherwise touched. One thing the user should know: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references at all, so the Background carries no citations and there was no art to draft around. As the brief warned, no prior-art search was run for this application, and the art available here is not merely possibly incomplete, it is empty. The claims were written from the disclosure alone and have not been tested against any reference. A search should be run before filing.
reasoning: The numeral checker's complaint about 4 and 5 was a real defect in the text, not a false positive in substance. Its regex consumes 'FIGS. 3' and then sees ', 4 and 5' as bare integers, which in a patent specification is exactly the pattern of an undefined reference numeral. Writing each figure reference out in full is the conservative fix: it satisfies the check and is also the more formal usage.

The FIG. 4 brief said the fragment was taken between the ledges so no ledge appears. That sentence existed to stop the renderer drawing a shelf into the wall, which is a renderer control rather than invention geometry. I replaced it with the affirmative fact the drawing actually needs, that the inner surface of the wall body is flat and continuous over the height of the fragment. Nothing about the ledges 18 changed; they remain shown in FIG. 3, where they carry the resilient feet 58.

I did not restructure the claim set or the description. The request was to write the draft and the reviewer found only mechanical faults, so widening the edit would have destroyed working text for nothing.

Claim 1 rests on the feature that carries the whole application: the depending indexing rib on the lid entering the mating channel of the spacer frame during closing travel and shifting the module into a registered position where the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages. That is the disclosed essential relationship, it does real technical work because the circulation path exists only when that overlap exists, and it is the alignment step that a passive carrier otherwise leaves to the packer. The full circulation path and the absence of any powered air mover are recited with it because the disclosure states both as essential.

Deliberately left out of claim 1: the compressible lid gasket, the resilient feet and ledges, the condensate channel, the wick and its pull tab, and the mechanical exposure indicator. The disclosure marks the wick and the indicator as optional, and the gasket and the retention feet, although disclosed as part of the closing sequence, are not needed for the registered path to exist. Each of them is a dependent claim instead, so the ladder retreats first to retention (claim 2), then sealing order (claim 3), then cassette geometry (claims 4 and 5), then condensate management (claims 6 to 8), then the irreversible indicator (claims 9 to 11), then the progressive registration travel (claim 12).

Three statutory hooks are claimed because three different parties infringe them: the assembled carrier (claim 1), the thermal module sold on its own as a replacement or refill item (claim 13, drafted with the shell, tray and lid in the preamble so the module itself is what is claimed), and the method of transporting goods (claim 17), which reaches the shipper who packs and closes the carrier.

Claim 17's first step recited peripheral outlet openings 'aligned with the side supply passages' while the passages were first introduced in the following step. That is a plain antecedent-basis defect. Deleting the phrase costs no scope, because the closing step later in the same claim recites the registered position in which the openings overlap the passages.

The 'is not drawn' and 'is omitted' sentences in the FIG. 2 and FIG. 6 briefs were doing legitimate work, telling the pipeline what is hidden, but they are phrased as absences. Since the same preflight rejected an absence-phrased instruction in FIG. 4, I rewrote them as statements of what conceals what and what the view contains, which is more robust and reads better on a sheet.
changes: draft/07-drawings.md: the FIG. 1 entry now refers to the enlarged regions as 'FIG. 3, in FIG. 4 and in FIG. 5' instead of 'FIGS. 3, 4 and 5', removing the bare integers the numeral check read as undefined reference numerals.
figures/FIG-1.md: same change to the sentence identifying the three broken-line regions.

figures/FIG-4.md: replaced 'This fragment is taken at a position along that wall between the ledges of the outer shell, so no ledge appears in this view' with a positive description of the wall body's flat inner surface running the height of the fragment.
figures/FIG-5.md: inserted the missing comma in the clause describing the thin upright wall spaced from the wall body, so the spacing and the lower-edge relationship read as two distinct facts.
figures/FIG-2.md: the concealed opening in the far long side wall is now described as concealed behind the second phase-change cassette 46 rather than as 'not drawn'.
figures/FIG-6.md: the closing sentence now states what the schematic detail view contains rather than what is omitted from it.

draft/09-claims.md: removed 'aligned with the side supply passages' from the first step of claim 17, where the side supply passages had no antecedent; the registered-position limitation later in the claim is unchanged.
input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there was no document to read, cite or draft around, and the Background contains no citation. That is not an omission on my part: there is nothing in the index to address, and inventing a citation is forbidden. The Background therefore states the problem in the inventor's own technical terms only, describing powered and passive carrier families generally, the payload temperature spread that results when a refrigerant mass is simply laid against the load, the dependence of any imposed circulation path on alignment a packer must produce by hand, the condensate that repeated opening leaves in a reusable carrier, and the fact that a recovered refrigerant erases the evidence of an excursion. Those four paragraphs are written so that a later argument has somewhere to stand: each one names a technical problem that a specific claimed feature solves, and the corresponding solution is explained in the Detailed Description before it is needed, in the same words the claims use. The distinguishing weight is placed on lid-driven registration, that is, the closing travel of the lid physically translating the thermal module into the position where the outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so that the alignment is produced by an act the packer cannot skip rather than by care or instructions. The secondary positions are the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator that reports the state of the refrigerant itself rather than an air-space sensor and that survives recovery of the cassette, and the wick in a condensate channel that is serviced by pulling a tab without opening or removing a cassette. Because no search was run, none of this has been measured against actual references, and the claims should be reassessed once a search exists.

structured_output.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there was no document to read, cite or draft around, and the Background contains no citation. That is not an omission on my part: there is nothing in the index to address, and inventing a citation is forbidden. The Background therefore states the problem in the inventor's own technical terms only, describing powered and passive carrier families generally, the payload temperature spread that results when a refrigerant mass is simply laid against the load, the dependence of any imposed circulation path on alignment a packer must produce by hand, the condensate that repeated opening leaves in a reusable carrier, and the fact that a recovered refrigerant erases the evidence of an excursion. Those four paragraphs are written so that a later argument has somewhere to stand: each one names a technical problem that a specific claimed feature solves, and the corresponding solution is explained in the Detailed Description before it is needed, in the same words the claims use. The distinguishing weight is placed on lid-driven registration, that is, the closing travel of the lid physically translating the thermal module into the position where the outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so that the alignment is produced by an act the packer cannot skip rather than by care or instructions. The secondary positions are the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator that reports the state of the refrigerant itself rather than an air-space sensor and that survives recovery of the cassette, and the wick in a condensate channel that is serviced by pulling a tab without opening or removing a cassette. Because no search was run, none of this has been measured against actual references, and the claims should be reassessed once a search exists.
structured_output.answer: The draft now passes the items the reviewer raised. The FIG. 4 brief no longer carries the negative instruction about the ledge and instead states positively that the inner surface of the wall body is flat and runs the full height of the fragment. While in the figure files I also repaired a run-on clause in the FIG. 5 brief and rephrased two hidden-structure sentences in FIG. 2 and FIG. 6 so they describe what conceals what rather than what is absent, and in the claims I removed a reference to the side supply passages that appeared in claim 17 one step before those passages were introduced. Everything else was left as it stood. Please note that prior_art/INDEX.md contains no references, so the application was drafted with no art to work around and no citations in the Background; a prior-art search should be run and the claims reviewed against it before filing.

In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.

The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12.

The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. The tray side walls 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.

The thermal module

Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 before packing.

The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, each guide duct 50 located beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 aligned with the side supply passages 28.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and the registration is completed by the closing of the lid. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is therefore created by an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 of the outer shell 10 lie beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. The resilient feet 58 maintain a downward holding force during transport, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.

The circulation path

In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Air warmed in the product region rises to the central inlet opening 48, and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes descends through the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, so that circulation proceeds without any powered air mover.

Condensate management

A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough formed in the outer shell 10 and extending around the product tray 20. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the condensate channel 70 and the absorbent wick 72 remain in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed. Discharge openings 76 are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

Mechanical exposure indicator

The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. Referring to FIG. 6, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.

Operation

In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. Goods are placed in the product tray 20 and the product tray 20 is placed in the outer shell 10 so that the tray feet 22 stand on the floor 12, leaving the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20 and the two side supply passages 28 between the tray side walls 26 and the side walls 14. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20. The insulated lid 60 is then closed, whereby the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 and shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position, the resilient feet 58 are pressed against the ledges 18 to retain the thermal module 40, and the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. Air thereafter circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover. At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.

Essential and optional features

Two phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42, opposed across the central space. Entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.

The described implementations are examples. A person skilled in the art may combine, substitute or omit the described features within the scope of the claims that follow.

# FIG. 5

Enlarged view of the condensate channel region of FIG. 1, seen horizontally in section. Plain black line work on white, diagonal section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

A thick hatched upright insulating wall body occupies the left portion of the drawing area, running from the upper part of the fragment down to a thick hatched horizontal bottom body that occupies the lower part and extends rightward.

In the upper right part of the drawing area, a hatched body fragment is drawn in section. An open vertical channel passes down through this fragment, bounded by hatched material to its left and right. This channel is one of the guide ducts 50. At the lower end of the channel, an opening passes through the downwardly facing bottom surface of the fragment. This opening is one of the discharge openings 76.

Below the body fragment, a thin hatched upright wall is drawn in section, spaced to the right of the inner surface of the upright wall body, its lower edge stopping short of the upwardly facing top surface of the horizontal bottom body above the trough described below. An open vertical space runs down between the upright wall body and the thin wall, from beneath the body fragment to the horizontal bottom body, so that the downward opening in the fragment stands above that space.

In the upwardly facing top surface of the horizontal bottom body, at the foot of the open vertical space and below the discharge opening 76, a shallow upwardly open trough is drawn in section, wider than it is deep. This trough is the condensate channel 70.

An elongated body of absorbent material lies in the trough, filling its lower part, shown schematically. This body is the absorbent wick 72. A narrow strip extends upward from its upper surface into the open vertical space, its free upper end clear of the surrounding surfaces. This strip is the pull tab 74.

- 50: inside the open vertical channel in the body fragment.
- 70: inside the trough at its left end, above the absorbent body.
- 72: well inside the elongated absorbent body lying in the trough.
- 74: well inside the narrow strip rising from the absorbent body.
- 76: on the opening through the bottom surface of the body fragment.

# FIG. 1

Schematic vertical sectional view of an assembled passive cold-chain carrier, taken on a vertical plane running transversely to the two upright blocks held within the module body and through the upwardly open groove in the top surface of that body. Plain black line work on white, section hatching on cut material, all line work inside the drawing area.

Two thick hatched upright wall bodies joined at the bottom by a thick hatched horizontal bottom body form an upright container, open at the top. These are the sectioned outer shell 10, its bottom body being the floor 12. A block with a flat upwardly facing top surface projects inward from each wall body below its top end.

A thick hatched horizontal slab across the top ends of both wall bodies is the insulated lid 60, closed. A narrow rib projects downward from its underside inboard of the left wall body top end, and a small compressible body lies between the slab and each top end.

Inside the container, a sectioned open-top box with thin hatched upright walls and a bottom wall is the product tray 20. Its bottom wall is raised above the floor 12 and its outer side surfaces stand clear of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap on each side. Small openings pass through each upright wall below the bottom wall level, and each upright wall stops short of the floor 12.

Two short hatched blocks between the tray bottom wall and the floor 12 are the tray feet 22. The open space between that wall and the floor 12 is the lower return passage 24. A shallow upwardly open trough at the foot of each gap holds an elongated absorbent body.

Between the open top of the product tray 20 and the lid 60, an elongated hatched body drawn in section is the thermal module 40. Two upright plain rectangular blocks, shown schematically, stand within it, spaced from one another and from its ends. The body is open downward at its centre. An open vertical channel runs down through the body outboard of each block, opening through its outboard side above the gap and opening again through its downwardly facing lower end above the trough beneath. A small block lies between the underside of the body and the flat top surface of each inward-projecting block of the wall bodies, contacting both and flattened between them. An upwardly open groove in the top surface of the body receives the lower end of the narrow rib.

Three thin broken-line closed curves are drawn. The first encloses the upper left region with the rib, the groove, the left wall top, the inward-projecting block of the left wall body and the small block resting on it. The second encloses the lower left region with the outboard channel opening, the left gap and the tray openings. The third encloses the lower end of the left channel with its downward opening, the trough and the absorbent body, and adjoins the second.

Each broken-line curve carries just outside it, clear of other line work, the designation of the view that enlarges it: FIG. 3 on the upper left curve, FIG. 4 on the lower left curve, and FIG. 5 on the curve at the trough. These designations are drawing annotation, not reference numerals.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 10: outside the container, with a lead line and arrow to the outer shell as a whole.
- 12: well inside the bottom body.
- 20: well inside the left upright wall of the box.
- 22: inside the left short block.
- 24: inside the space beneath the tray bottom wall.
- 40: outside the container, with a lead line and arrow to the module as a whole.
- 60: well inside the slab at the top.
- 100: outside the container, with a lead line and arrow to the whole carrier.

A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the condensate channel 70 and the absorbent wick 72 remain in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

Condensate management

A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough extending around the product tray 20. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the condensate channel 70 and the absorbent wick 72 remain in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed. Discharge openings 76 are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

# FIG. 5

Enlarged view of the condensate channel region of FIG. 1, seen horizontally in section. Plain black line work on white, diagonal section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

A thick hatched upright insulating wall body occupies the left portion of the drawing area, running from the upper part of the fragment down to a thick hatched horizontal bottom body that occupies the lower part and extends rightward.

In the upper right part of the drawing area, a hatched body fragment is drawn in section. An open vertical channel passes down through this fragment, bounded by hatched material to its left and right. This channel is one of the guide ducts 50. At the lower end of the channel, an opening passes through the downwardly facing bottom surface of the fragment. This opening is one of the discharge openings 76.

Below the body fragment, a thin hatched upright wall is drawn in section, spaced to the right of the inner surface of the upright wall body, its lower edge stopping short of the upwardly facing top surface of the horizontal bottom body above the trough described below. A series of small openings passes through this thin upright wall, as in FIG. 1 and FIG. 4. In the upwardly facing top surface of the horizontal bottom body, at the foot of the open vertical space and below the discharge opening 76, a shallow upwardly open trough is drawn in section, wider than it is deep. This trough is the condensate channel 70.

An elongated body of absorbent material lies in the trough, filling its lower part, shown schematically. This body is the absorbent wick 72. content.text:
All six findings are fixed and the files are back in sync.

- **Condensate channel wording** — `draft/08-detailed-description.md` now reads "A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough extending around the product tray 20." The following sentence already carries the supported fact that the channel and wick remain in the outer shell when the tray is removed, so nothing else moved. Claims 6, 16 and 19 and the figure briefs are untouched.
- **FIG. 1 missing the resilient-foot bearing** — the FIG. 1 brief now draws a small block flattened between the module body underside and the flat top surface of each inward-projecting block of the wall bodies, and the upper left broken-line curve encloses that block and the projection it rests on. Those parts stay unnumbered on FIG. 1 (58 and 18 are labelled on FIG. 3), so they are described generically there.
- **FIG. 1 missing the duct-end discharge opening** — each vertical channel in the module body now opens both through the outboard side above the gap and through its downwardly facing lower end above the trough, and the third curve encloses that lower end, its downward opening, the trough and the absorbent body, adjoining the FIG. 4 curve.
- **FIG. 5 tray wall without perforations** — the thin upright wall in FIG. 5 now carries the same series of small openings shown in FIG. 1 and FIG. 4. No numeral was added to FIG. 5.
- **Curve designations** — FIG. 1 carries FIG. 3, FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 just outside the respective curves, and the Brief Description now sends the reader to "the broken-line curve there designated FIG. 3/4/5", with matching opening sentences in the three enlargement briefs. The designations are listed under a separate "View designations" heading, not in the reference-numeral list and not in `numerals.md`, because a view designation is drawing annotation rather than a numeral.
- **Cutting planes** — FIG. 1 is now stated to be taken on a vertical plane cutting transversely through the two phase-change cassettes and through the mating channel, and FIG. 6 on a horizontal plane through the mechanical exposure indicator and a wall of the outer shell, in both the Brief Description and the briefs.

FIG. 1 had to be rewritten compactly to hold the new structure within the brief length limit; every body, contact and opening previously specified is still there, and its numeral list is unchanged.

input.summary: All six review findings are fixed. The description no longer asserts that the condensate channel is formed in the outer shell, which was a structural claim the disclosure does not make. FIG. 1 now depicts the two things its own enlargements showed but it did not: the small block flattened between the module body and each inward-projecting wall block, and the downward opening at the lower end of each vertical channel above the trough. Its three broken-line curves were redrawn to enclose that structure, and they now carry the designations FIG. 3, FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 so each region is tied to the view that enlarges it. FIG. 5 now shows the same series of small openings in the tray side wall that FIG. 1 and FIG. 4 show. Both sectional views state their cutting plane in words, in the Brief Description and in the briefs, since no view in the set could carry a section line for FIG. 1. FIG. 1 was rewritten compactly to hold the added structure inside the brief length limit; no body, contact or opening was dropped in doing so, and its numeral list is unchanged. The claims, the numeral table and the disclosed embodiments were not altered.
reasoning: The condensate finding was correct and mattered. The inventor says only that the wick lies in a shallow condensate channel around the product tray, and that the pull tab stays reachable once the tray is out. That supports the channel staying behind with the shell, which is what claims 16 and 19 recite, but it does not support the channel being integral with the shell. I deleted 'formed in the outer shell 10' and left the next sentence, which already says the channel and wick remain in the outer shell when the tray is removed, so no support was lost and no redundancy was added. The trough drawn in the floor body stays a drawing convention confined to the FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 briefs.

For the two cross-view findings I fixed the parent view, not the enlargements. Both the foot bearing on the ledge and the discharge opening at the duct lower end are affirmatively disclosed, so removing them from FIG. 3 and FIG. 5 would have deleted disclosed structure to buy consistency. FIG. 1 gained them instead.

On FIG. 1 those parts are described without their canonical names or numerals, as a small block, an inward-projecting block, and an opening through the downwardly facing lower end of the channel. Numerals 58, 18 and 76 belong to FIG. 3 and FIG. 5, and repeating their part names on a sheet that does not list them would create the mismatch the numeral rules forbid.

Adding that structure pushed the FIG. 1 brief well past the length limit, so I compressed the prose rather than dropping content. Every solid, contact, gap, opening and curve that was specified before is still specified; what went was verbosity, for example merging the shell and lid paragraphs and shortening the numeral endpoint phrasing. The eight numerals on the sheet are unchanged.

The curve designations are placed under a separate View designations heading rather than in the reference-numeral list. A designation identifying an enlarged view is annotation that the pipeline adds deterministically, and putting FIG. 3 into a numeral list would misrepresent it as a reference numeral and pollute numerals.md.

For the cutting planes I used words rather than section lines. FIG. 2 is a perspective of the module alone and FIG. 3 to FIG. 6 are enlargements, so there is no view from which FIG. 1's plane could be cut and no honest place to put an arrowed section line. FIG. 1's own content fixes the plane, so stating it adds no new matter.

While in the briefs I broadened three leader endpoints that carried placement modifiers with no basis in the disclosure: numeral 70 now targets the trough interior clear of the absorbent body rather than its left end, 42 targets the frame body clear of the groove rather than a quadrant of it, and 80 targets the indicator outline clear of the shaft rather than its left part. Each still distinguishes the intended part from its neighbour, which is the only reason to constrain an endpoint at all.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md still lists no references, so there is nothing to cite, nothing to distinguish in the Background, and no reference vocabulary to avoid. The Background therefore carries no citation and states the problem in the inventor's own technical terms: the temperature spread that results when a refrigerant mass is simply laid against a payload, the fact that any imposed circulation path depends on an alignment a packer must produce by hand, the condensate that repeated opening leaves in a reusable carrier, and the erasure of an excursion once the refrigerant recovers. Each of those paragraphs states the technical problem that a specific claimed feature solves, and the corresponding solution appears in the Detailed Description in the same words the claims use, which is what a later argument would be built from. The distinguishing weight sits on lid-driven registration: the closing travel of the lid physically translating the thermal module until the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so the alignment the passive circulation path depends on is produced by an act the packer cannot skip. Secondary positions are the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator, which reports the state of the refrigerant itself and survives its recovery, and the wick in a condensate channel serviced by a pull tab without opening or removing a cassette. Nothing this turn changed claim scope. Because no search was run, none of this has been measured against real references, and a search should be run before filing.

structured_output.summary: All six review findings are fixed. The description no longer asserts that the condensate channel is formed in the outer shell, which was a structural claim the disclosure does not make. FIG. 1 now depicts the two things its own enlargements showed but it did not: the small block flattened between the module body and each inward-projecting wall block, and the downward opening at the lower end of each vertical channel above the trough. Its three broken-line curves were redrawn to enclose that structure, and they now carry the designations FIG. 3, FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 so each region is tied to the view that enlarges it. FIG. 5 now shows the same series of small openings in the tray side wall that FIG. 1 and FIG. 4 show. Both sectional views state their cutting plane in words, in the Brief Description and in the briefs, since no view in the set could carry a section line for FIG. 1. FIG. 1 was rewritten compactly to hold the added structure inside the brief length limit; no body, contact or opening was dropped in doing so, and its numeral list is unchanged. The claims, the numeral table and the disclosed embodiments were not altered.
reasoning: The condensate finding was correct and mattered. The inventor says only that the wick lies in a shallow condensate channel around the product tray, and that the pull tab stays reachable once the tray is out. That supports the channel staying behind with the shell, which is what claims 16 and 19 recite, but it does not support the channel being integral with the shell. I deleted 'formed in the outer shell 10' and left the next sentence, which already says the channel and wick remain in the outer shell when the tray is removed, so no support was lost and no redundancy was added. The trough drawn in the floor body stays a drawing convention confined to the FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 briefs.

For the two cross-view findings I fixed the parent view, not the enlargements. Both the foot bearing on the ledge and the discharge opening at the duct lower end are affirmatively disclosed, so removing them from FIG. 3 and FIG. 5 would have deleted disclosed structure to buy consistency. FIG. 1 gained them instead.

On FIG. 1 those parts are described without their canonical names or numerals, as a small block, an inward-projecting block, and an opening through the downwardly facing lower end of the channel. Numerals 58, 18 and 76 belong to FIG. 3 and FIG. 5, and repeating their part names on a sheet that does not list them would create the mismatch the numeral rules forbid.

Adding that structure pushed the FIG. 1 brief well past the length limit, so I compressed the prose rather than dropping content. Every solid, contact, gap, opening and curve that was specified before is still specified; what went was verbosity, for example merging the shell and lid paragraphs and shortening the numeral endpoint phrasing. The eight numerals on the sheet are unchanged.

The curve designations are placed under a separate View designations heading rather than in the reference-numeral list. A designation identifying an enlarged view is annotation that the pipeline adds deterministically, and putting FIG. 3 into a numeral list would misrepresent it as a reference numeral and pollute numerals.md.

For the cutting planes I used words rather than section lines. FIG. 2 is a perspective of the module alone and FIG. 3 to FIG. 6 are enlargements, so there is no view from which FIG. 1's plane could be cut and no honest place to put an arrowed section line. FIG. 1's own content fixes the plane, so stating it adds no new matter.

While in the briefs I broadened three leader endpoints that carried placement modifiers with no basis in the disclosure: numeral 70 now targets the trough interior clear of the absorbent body rather than its left end, 42 targets the frame body clear of the groove rather than a quadrant of it, and 80 targets the indicator outline clear of the shaft rather than its left part. Each still distinguishes the intended part from its neighbour, which is the only reason to constrain an endpoint at all.

(major, internal_logic) The FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 enlargement regions are placed as adjoining curves on the same left side of FIG. 1, but the two briefs enclose the same left-hand vertical corridor over the same elevation range - FIG. 4 runs from the module's outboard outlet opening down to the lower return passage at the floor, and FIG. 5 runs from the module's downward discharge opening down to the trough at the floor. Two adjoining, non-overlapping curves cannot enclose both.

2. (major, internal_logic) FIG-6.md adds an "upright plain rectangular block … This block is the first phase-change cassette 44" directly inboard of side wall 14 with the indicator stem's inner end touching it. The FIG. 6 entry in 07-drawings.md lists only the stem, latch and spring. The geometry also contradicts FIG. 2 and FIG. 3, where cassette 44 is separated from the shell side wall by a guide duct, the frame's long side wall and the side supply passage, and it implies a stem crossing side supply passage 28 - contrary to claim 11 and to the statement that the indicator "neither opens, closes nor throttles … the side supply passages 28".

3. (major, formalities) FIG. 6 is designated a sectional view "taken on a horizontal plane through the mechanical exposure indicator and a wall of the outer shell", but no view carries a cutting-plane line, and the plane is described in words rather than by a repeated designation, unlike the properly designated FIG. 3/4/5 enlargement curves. (FIG. 1's word-described plane is acceptable because no view of the assembled carrier exists from which to cut it.)

4. (minor, internal_logic) Claims 1 and 13 recite the peripheral outlet openings as already "aligned with the side supply passages" in the module element while the same claims require the indexing rib to shift the module into the registered position "in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages". The description carries the same double statement.

5. (minor, formalities) FIG-1.md states that the section plane cuts "through both upright blocks within the module body" and that hatching is applied to cut material, yet draws those blocks "plain".

Note on scope: the drafting brief records that no prior-art search was run, so the art on file may be incomplete; that is outside this preflight, and Background characterisations are traced by the later citation review.

## Mechanical checks that did not pass

- **Source fidelity is clean before rendering** (fail): SOURCE LEDGER - RESULT

The substantive ledger traces clean. Every claim limitation, every numbered part (10, 12, 14, 18, 20, 22, 24, 26, 28, 30, 40, 42, 44, 46, 48, 50, 54, 56, 58, 60, 62, 64, 70, 72, 74, 76, 80, 82, 84, 86, 100), and every structure, relationship, result and variant in the Summary, Detailed Description and figure briefs traces to an affirmative USER passage in input/disclosure.md, which is reproduced verbatim as the single USER turn in input/conversation.md. Spot-checks: shell/tray/module/lid and tray feet with lower return passage and two side supply passages ("The product tray is suspended above the shell floor by feet so that a lower return passage remains under the tray. The tray side walls are spaced inward from the shell side walls to form two side supply passages."); spacer frame with central inlet, two downward guide ducts, peripheral outlet openings, and the full circulation path ("Warm air rising from the product region enters the central inlet, divides along faces of the cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage."); passivity ("It has no fan, pump, or powered air mover."); lid-driven registration, gasket-after-registration and resilient-feet/ledge retention (disclosure ¶9); condensate channel, wick, discharge openings and pull tab (¶11); mechanical exposure indicator with stem, temperature-responsive latch, spring, latched exposed position, manual reset only after opening, and no airflow control (¶13); method steps (¶15); optional status of wick and indicator ("The wick and the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator are supported optional features."). Dependent claims 2–12, 14–16 and 18–20 each map to one of those passages. Title, "Not applicable" cross-reference and "Not applicable" government-support statement match input/brief.md ("No priority claim. No federally sponsored research or development."). B
  - FIG. 1's FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 enlargement curves enclose the same region
  - FIG. 6 adds phase-change cassette 44 against the shell wall, contradicting FIG. 2, FIG. 3 and claim 11
  - FIG. 6 is designated a sectional view but no view carries the corresponding section line
  - Outlet openings recited as already aligned and as brought into overlap by registration

## Reviewer findings

- **[major] FIG. 1's FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 enlargement curves enclose the same region** (figures/FIG-1.md line 11; figures/FIG-4.md; figures/FIG-5.md) - FIG. 1 places both lower enlargement curves on the left side as adjoining regions, but the two enlargement briefs cover the same left-hand vertical corridor across the same elevation range, so the curves cannot be distinct and adjoining. FIG. 4 must reach from the module's outboard outlet opening down to the lower return passage at the floor, and FIG. 5 must reach from the module's downward discharge opening (at the same module level) down to the trough at the floor. Each therefore spans module-bottom to floor on the left side, and each redundantly encloses the tray side wall, its small openings and the side supply passage. As specified, the two broken-line curves would overlap almost entirely rather than adjoin, and a reader could not tell which enlargement belongs to which region.
  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-1.md line 11, replace "and one adjoining it around the left channel lower end, its downward opening, the trough and absorbent body" with "and one at the lower right around the right channel lower end, its downward opening, the trough and absorbent body"; in the "View designations" list change "FIG. 5: outside the curve at the trough." to "FIG. 5: outside the lower right curve." In figures/FIG-5.md, mirror the fragment so the thick hatched upright insulating wall body and the horizontal bottom body lie at the right of the drawing area, the body fragment at the upper left, and the thin tray side wall spaced to the left of the shell wall's inner surface, leaving every numeral and every named element unchanged. No text in draft/07-drawings.md or draft/08-detailed-description.md changes, since neither states a side for FIG. 4 or FIG. 5.
- **[major] FIG. 6 adds phase-change cassette 44 against the shell wall, contradicting FIG. 2, FIG. 3 and claim 11** (figures/FIG-6.md lines 15 and 21; draft/07-drawings.md line 11) - The FIG. 6 brief places an upright block identified as the first phase-change cassette 44 in open space immediately inboard of side wall 14, with the inner end of indicator stem 82 adjacent its face, and labels it. Three inconsistencies follow. (a) The FIG. 6 entry in the Brief Description lists only the indicator stem, the temperature-responsive latch and the spring, so the brief depicts and numbers an element the drawing description does not name. (b) The placement contradicts FIG. 2 and FIG. 3: FIG. 2 holds cassette 44 spaced inward from the frame's near long side wall with a guide duct between them, and FIG. 3 shows spacer frame 42 spaced inward from side wall 14, so a horizontal section through wall 14 at module height must show the side supply passage, the frame's long side wall and the guide duct between wall 14 and cassette 44, not open space. (c) A stem running horizontally from outside the shell into contact with cassette 44 would cross side supply passage 28, contrary to claim 11 and to the description's statement that the indicator does not throttle the side supply passages. The disclosure states only that the stem is "thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette" and gives no coupling geometry.
  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-6.md, delete line 15 in its entirety ("In the open space at the right of the drawing area, an upright plain rectangular block is drawn, shown schematically, its left face adjacent the inner end of the shaft. This block is the first phase-change cassette 44. This schematic detail view shows the wall body, the indicator body with its shaft, spring and latch, and this block.") and delete the numeral entry "- 44: well inside the upright rectangular block at the right." In line 9, replace "its inner end reaches into the open space at the right of the drawing area" with "its inner end projects past the inner surface of the wall body". Numeral 44 remains shown on FIG. 2, and the thermal coupling remains stated in draft/08-detailed-description.md ("The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44."); no other text changes.
- **[major] FIG. 6 is designated a sectional view but no view carries the corresponding section line** (draft/07-drawings.md line 11; figures/FIG-6.md line 3; figures/FIG-1.md "View designations") - FIG. 6 is presented as a section taken on a stated cutting plane, but that plane is nowhere indicated on any view, and no repeated designation ties the sectional view to a source view. The three enlargements are handled correctly by comparison: FIG. 1 carries broken-line curves designated FIG. 3, FIG. 4 and FIG. 5, and each enlargement brief and the Brief Description repeat the same designation. FIG. 6 alone is a hatched section whose plane cuts structure that is shown elsewhere (side wall 14, shown in FIG. 1 and FIG. 3), so the plane can and should be indicated. As drafted, the FIG. 6 designation chain has no source-view member at all.
  - Suggested fix: Add the indicator and its section line to FIG. 1 and repeat the designation in all three places. In figures/FIG-1.md, add to the body: "Within the left wall body, below the inward-projecting block, a horizontally elongated plain rectangular outline extends through the wall thickness with a shaft projecting out past its outer surface; this is the mechanical exposure indicator 80. A horizontal broken line with a short arrow at each end crosses the left wall body at the level of that outline, each end designated 6."; add "- 80: on the outline in the left wall body." to "Numerals shown on this figure"; and add "- 6-6: at each end of the horizontal broken line across the left wall body." to "View designations". In draft/07-drawings.md line 11, replace "taken on a horizontal plane through the mechanical exposure indicator and a wall of the outer shell" with "taken on line 6-6 of FIG. 1". In figures/FIG-6.md line 3, make the same replacement.
- **[minor] Outlet openings recited as already aligned and as brought into overlap by registration** (draft/09-claims.md claims 1 and 13; draft/06-summary.md line 3; draft/08-detailed-description.md line 15) - Each independent apparatus claim recites the peripheral outlet openings as structurally "aligned with the side supply passages" as a property of the thermal module, and in the same claim requires the indexing rib to shift the module into a registered position "in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages". If the openings are already aligned, the registration limitation is met before the lid closes; the two recitations pull against each other. The wording mirrors the disclosure, which uses "aligned" descriptively rather than as a pre-registration structural state, so the fix is a wording change only and narrows nothing.
  - Suggested fix: In draft/09-claims.md claim 1, replace "peripheral outlet openings aligned with the side supply passages" with "peripheral outlet openings positioned to align with the side supply passages"; make the identical replacement in claim 13. In draft/06-summary.md line 3 and draft/08-detailed-description.md line 15, replace "peripheral outlet openings aligned with the side supply passages 28" (and the corresponding Summary phrase "and peripheral outlet openings" already reads correctly) with "peripheral outlet openings positioned to align with the side supply passages 28".
- **[minor] FIG. 1 draws the sectioned cassette blocks unhatched though the stated plane cuts them** (figures/FIG-1.md lines 3 and 9) - The FIG. 1 brief states that the cutting plane passes through both upright blocks within the module body and that hatching is applied to cut material, yet it then specifies those blocks as plain rectangles with no hatching. The two instructions in the same brief conflict, and the resulting view would show cut material without section lining while every other cut body in the same view is hatched.
  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-1.md line 9, replace "Two upright plain rectangular blocks, shown schematically, stand within it" with "Two upright hatched rectangular blocks, shown schematically, stand within it".

Fix every listed item before returning. If an advisory is a false positive, make
the wording or figure specification unambiguous enough that the check passes.

an insulated outer shell having a floor, side walls and an upper edge;

a thermal module removably received in the outer shell above the product tray, the thermal module comprising a rigid spacer frame and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame, the spacer frame defining a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts located beside the phase-change cassettes, peripheral outlet openings aligned with the side supply passages, and a mating channel; and

an insulated lid closable on the upper edge of the outer shell and carrying a depending indexing rib positioned to enter the mating channel as the insulated lid closes and to shift the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages;

the carrier being free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover, and the outer shell, the product tray, the thermal module and the insulated lid cooperating in the registered position to define a circulation path along which air rising from a product region within the product tray enters the central inlet opening, divides along faces of the two phase-change cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through the perforations, and returns through the lower return passage.

placing the goods in a product tray and placing the product tray in an insulated outer shell so that tray feet of the product tray stand on a floor of the outer shell, leaving a lower return passage between the product tray and the floor and two side supply passages between tray side walls of the product tray and side walls of the outer shell;

In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.

The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12.

The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. The tray side walls 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.

The thermal module

Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 before packing.

The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, each guide duct 50 located beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 aligned with the side supply passages 28.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and the registration is completed by the closing of the lid. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is therefore created by an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 of the outer shell 10 lie beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. The resilient feet 58 maintain a downward holding force during transport, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.

The circulation path

In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Air warmed in the product region rises to the central inlet opening 48, and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes descends through the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, so that circulation proceeds without any powered air mover.

Condensate management

A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough extending around the product tray 20. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the condensate channel 70 and the absorbent wick 72 remain in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed. Discharge openings 76 are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

Mechanical exposure indicator

The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. Referring to FIG. 6, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.

Operation

In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. Goods are placed in the product tray 20 and the product tray 20 is placed in the outer shell 10 so that the tray feet 22 stand on the floor 12, leaving the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20 and the two side supply passages 28 between the tray side walls 26 and the side walls 14. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20. The insulated lid 60 is then closed, whereby the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 and shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position, the resilient feet 58 are pressed against the ledges 18 to retain the thermal module 40, and the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. Air thereafter circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover. At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.

Essential and optional features

Two phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42, opposed across the central space. Entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.

The described implementations are examples. A person skilled in the art may combine, substitute or omit the described features within the scope of the claims that follow.

# FIG. 1

Schematic vertical section of an assembled passive cold-chain carrier, on a plane cutting through both upright blocks within the module body and the groove in its top surface. Plain black line work on white, hatching on cut material, all inside the drawing area.

Two thick hatched upright wall bodies and a thick hatched bottom body joining them form an upright container open at the top: the sectioned outer shell 10, its bottom body the floor 12. Below its top end each wall body carries an inward-projecting block with a flat top surface. A thick hatched horizontal slab across both top ends is the insulated lid 60, closed, a narrow rib projecting down from its underside inboard of the left top end and a small compressible body between it and each top end.

Within it, a sectioned open-top box with thin hatched walls and a bottom wall is the product tray 20, standing above the floor 12 on two short hatched blocks, the tray feet 22, the space beneath it being the lower return passage 24. Its walls stand clear of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap each side, stop short of the floor 12, and carry small openings below bottom wall level. A shallow upwardly open trough at the foot of each gap holds an elongated absorbent body.

Above the product tray 20 and below the lid 60 is an elongated hatched body in section, the thermal module 40, open downward at its centre. Two upright plain rectangular blocks, shown schematically, stand within it, spaced apart and from its ends. An open vertical channel runs down outboard of each block, opening through the body's outboard side above the gap and through its downwardly facing lower end above the trough. A small block, flattened between them, lies between the body underside and each inward-projecting block top surface. A groove opening upward in the top surface receives the lower end of the narrow rib.

Three broken-line curves are drawn: one at the upper left around the rib, groove, left wall top, left inward-projecting block and the small block on it; one at the lower left around the left outboard channel opening, left gap and tray openings; and one adjoining it around the left channel lower end, its downward opening, the trough and absorbent body.

Enlarged view of the condensate channel region of FIG. 1 enclosed by the broken-line curve there designated FIG. 5, seen horizontally in section. Plain black line work on white, diagonal section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

A thick hatched upright insulating wall body occupies the left portion of the drawing area, running from the upper part of the fragment down to a thick hatched horizontal bottom body that occupies the lower part and extends rightward.

In the upper right part of the drawing area, a hatched body fragment is drawn in section. An open vertical channel passes down through this fragment, bounded by hatched material to its left and right. This channel is one of the guide ducts 50. At the lower end of the channel, an opening passes through the downwardly facing bottom surface of the fragment. This opening is one of the discharge openings 76.

Below the body fragment, a thin hatched upright wall is drawn in section, spaced to the right of the inner surface of the upright wall body, its lower edge stopping short of the upwardly facing top surface of the horizontal bottom body above the trough described below. A series of small openings passes through this thin upright wall, as in FIG. 1 and FIG. 4. An open vertical space runs down between the upright wall body and the thin wall, from beneath the body fragment to the horizontal bottom body, so that the downward opening in the fragment stands above that space.

In the upwardly facing top surface of the horizontal bottom body, at the foot of the open vertical space and below the discharge opening 76, a shallow upwardly open trough is drawn in section, wider than it is deep. This trough is the condensate channel 70.

An elongated body of absorbent material lies in the trough, filling its lower part, shown schematically. This body is the absorbent wick 72. A narrow strip extends upward from its upper surface into the open vertical space, its free upper end clear of the surrounding surfaces. This strip is the pull tab 74.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 50: inside the open vertical channel in the body fragment.
- 70: inside the trough, clear of the absorbent body.
- 72: well inside the elongated absorbent body lying in the trough.
- 74: well inside the narrow strip rising from the absorbent body.
- 76: on the opening through the bottom surface of the body fragment.
