# FIG. 7

Enlarged schematic sectional view of the mechanical exposure indicator, taken on line 7-7 of FIG. 6, with the indicator stem in the exposed position. Plain black line work on white, section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

A thick hatched upright wall body stands across the middle of the drawing area, its outer surface facing left and its inner surface facing right. This wall body is one of the side walls 14 of the sectioned outer shell 10.

Carried by the wall body, and drawn as a horizontally elongated plain rectangular outline extending through the thickness of the wall body from its outer surface to its inner surface, is the body of the mechanical exposure indicator 80, shown schematically and open at both of its ends.

An elongated horizontal shaft lies within that outline and extends beyond both of its ends: to the left the shaft projects past the outer surface of the wall body, and to the right its inner end projects past the inner surface of the wall body. This shaft is the indicator stem 82.

A coil spring surrounds the shaft within the outline, drawn as aligned loops and shown extended, its loops spaced apart. This spring is the spring 86.

A small block sits above the shaft within the outline, to the right of the coil spring, projecting downward with its lower end adjacent the upper surface of the shaft, shown schematically. This block is the temperature-responsive latch 84.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 10: outside the wall body, clear of line work, with a lead line and arrow to the outer shell as a whole.
- 14: well inside the hatching of the upright wall body, below the indicator outline.
- 80: on the outline of the indicator body carried by the wall body, clear of the shaft.
- 82: on the part of the shaft projecting left beyond the outer surface of the wall body.
- 84: well inside the small block above the shaft.
- 86: on one loop of the coil spring surrounding the shaft.

In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.

The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12.

The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. The tray side walls 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.

The thermal module

Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 before packing.

The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, each guide duct 50 located beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 positioned to align with the side supply passages 28.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and the registration is completed by the closing of the lid. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is therefore created by an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 of the outer shell 10 lie beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. The resilient feet 58 maintain a downward holding force during transport, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.

The circulation path

In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Air warmed in the product region rises to the central inlet opening 48, and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes descends through the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, so that circulation proceeds without any powered air mover.

Condensate management

A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough extending around the product tray 20. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the condensate channel 70 and the absorbent wick 72 remain in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed. Discharge openings 76 are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

Mechanical exposure indicator

The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. Referring to FIG. 6, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.

Operation

In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. Goods are placed in the product tray 20 and the product tray 20 is placed in the outer shell 10 so that the tray feet 22 stand on the floor 12, leaving the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20 and the two side supply passages 28 between the tray side walls 26 and the side walls 14. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20. The insulated lid 60 is then closed, whereby the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 and shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position, the resilient feet 58 are pressed against the ledges 18 to retain the thermal module 40, and the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. Air thereafter circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover. At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.

Essential and optional features

Two phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42, opposed across the central space. Entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.

The described implementations are examples. A person skilled in the art may combine, substitute or omit the described features within the scope of the claims that follow.

# FIG. 1

Schematic vertical section of an assembled passive cold-chain carrier, on a plane cutting through both upright blocks within the module body and the groove in its top surface. Plain black line work on white, hatching on cut material, all inside the drawing area.

Two thick hatched upright wall bodies and a thick hatched bottom body joining them form an upright container open at the top: the sectioned outer shell 10, its bottom body the floor 12. Below its top end each wall body carries an inward-projecting block with a flat top surface. A thick hatched horizontal slab across both top ends is the insulated lid 60, closed, a narrow rib projecting down from its underside inboard of the left top end and a small compressible body between it and each top end.

Within it, a sectioned open-top box with thin hatched walls and a bottom wall is the product tray 20, standing above the floor 12 on two short hatched blocks, the tray feet 22, the space beneath it being the lower return passage 24. Its walls stand clear of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap each side, stop short of the floor 12, and carry small openings below bottom wall level. A shallow upwardly open trough at the foot of each gap holds an elongated absorbent body.

Above the product tray 20 and below the lid 60 is an elongated hatched body in section, the thermal module 40, open downward at its centre. Two upright hatched rectangular blocks, shown schematically, stand within it, spaced apart and from its ends. An open vertical channel runs down outboard of each block, opening through the body's outboard side above the gap and through its downwardly facing lower end above the trough. A small block, flattened between them, lies between the body underside and each inward-projecting block top surface. A groove opening upward in the top surface receives the lower end of the narrow rib.

Three broken-line curves are drawn: one at the upper left around the rib, groove, left wall top, left inward-projecting block and the small block on it; one at the lower left around the left outboard channel opening, left gap and tray openings; and one at the lower right around the right channel lower end, its downward opening, the right trough and absorbent body.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 10: outside the container, lead line to the shell.
- 12: well inside the bottom body.
- 20: well inside the left tray wall.
- 22: well inside the left short block.
- 24: inside the space beneath the tray bottom wall.
- 40: outside the container, lead line to the module.
- 60: well inside the top slab.
- 100: outside the container, lead line to the carrier.

## View designations

- FIG. 3: outside the upper left curve.
- FIG. 4: outside the lower left curve.
- FIG. 5: outside the lower right curve.

All five findings are fixed and the figure set is re-synchronized.

- **Overlapping enlargement regions** — the FIG. 5 region now sits at the lower right of FIG. 1 (right channel lower end, its downward opening, the right trough and absorbent body), so it no longer competes with the lower left FIG. 4 region. `figures/FIG-5.md` is mirrored to match: shell wall and bottom body at the right, module fragment at the upper left, tray wall spaced to the left of the shell wall's inner surface. Every numeral and named element on that sheet is unchanged.
- **Cassette against the shell wall in the indicator detail** — the upright block identified as cassette 44 and its numeral entry are gone, and the stem's inner end is now described as projecting past the inner surface of the wall body. Numeral 44 remains on FIG. 2, and the thermal coupling remains stated in the Detailed Description, where the disclosure puts it.
- **Section line for the indicator view** — FIG. 6 is now a fragmentary elevation of the outside of the shell at the indicator, showing the indicator visible from outside and the outer end of the stem, and carrying a broken cutting-plane line with an arrow at each end pointing toward the bottom of the drawing area and the repeated designation, reading line 7-7. The indicator section becomes FIG. 7, taken on line 7-7 of FIG. 6. The Brief Description and the Detailed Description follow. I put the source view on its own sheet rather than on FIG. 1 because FIG. 1 is already at eight numerals and at the brief length ceiling, so adding the indicator and the cutting line there would have overcrowded it.
- **Aligned versus brought into overlap** — claims 1 and 13 and the Detailed Description now recite the peripheral outlet openings as "positioned to align with the side supply passages", leaving the overlap to the registration limitation. No scope narrowed.
- **Unhatched cassette blocks in FIG. 1** — the two upright blocks the stated plane cuts are now hatched like every other cut body in that view.

Figure briefs all remain under the length limit, and the numeral table needed no change: every numeral is still defined once and appears on at least one sheet.

input.summary: All five findings are fixed. The FIG. 5 enlargement region moves to the lower right of FIG. 1 and the FIG. 5 brief is mirrored to the right side of the carrier, so the two lower enlargement curves cover different corridors instead of the same one. The phase-change cassette block that the indicator detail placed against the shell wall is deleted along with its numeral entry, and the stem's inner end is now described only as projecting past the inner surface of the wall body, which removes the conflict with FIG. 2, FIG. 3 and claim 11. The indicator section now has a source view: a new fragmentary elevation of the outside of the shell at the indicator, FIG. 6, carries a broken cutting-plane line with arrows and the repeated designation reading line 7-7, and the indicator section becomes FIG. 7 taken on line 7-7 of FIG. 6, with the Brief Description and Detailed Description synchronized. Claims 1 and 13 and the matching description sentence now say the peripheral outlet openings are positioned to align with the side supply passages, so the structural recitation no longer pre-empts the registration limitation. The two upright blocks that FIG. 1's stated plane cuts are now hatched like the other cut bodies. The numeral table is unchanged and every numeral still appears on at least one sheet.
reasoning: The overlap finding was a geometry error I introduced last turn when I made the FIG. 5 region adjoin the FIG. 4 region on the same side. Both enlargements run from module level down to the floor in the same side corridor, so they can only be distinct if they are taken on opposite sides of the carrier. Moving FIG. 5 to the right and mirroring its brief keeps every disclosed part on that sheet and needs no change to the Brief Description or the description, neither of which states a side.

For the indicator detail I deleted the cassette block rather than reconciling the geometry, because the disclosure says only that the stem is thermally coupled to one cassette and gives no coupling geometry. Drawing the cassette in open space against the shell wall was the figure inventing a path that would have had to cross the side supply passage, contradicting the claim that the indicator does not throttle those passages. The thermal coupling stays where the disclosure puts it, in the description.

The section-line finding needed a source view, and I gave FIG. 6 its own rather than adding the indicator and a cutting line to FIG. 1. FIG. 1 already carries the maximum eight numerals and sits within a few characters of the brief length ceiling, so the additions would have forced disclosed geometry off that sheet, which is exactly what the figure-plan rule forbids. A fragmentary exterior elevation is also the honest source view here: it needs no cutting plane of its own, and it shows the disclosed fact that the indicator is visible from outside the carrier.

That choice renumbers the indicator section to FIG. 7 so the source view precedes the section taken from it. The Brief Description gains a FIG. 6 entry and a FIG. 7 entry, and the one description paragraph that referred to FIG. 6 now names FIG. 6 for the outside appearance and FIG. 7 for the sectioned mechanism. Nothing about the indicator itself changed.

The cutting line is specified the way a section line has to be: broken, horizontal, both physical endpoints given, an arrow at each end pointing toward the bottom of the drawing area so the section reads as seen looking down, and the same designation repeated at both ends so the line reads 7-7. The designation is listed under View designations, not in the numeral list and not in numerals.md, because it is drawing annotation rather than a reference numeral.

On the aligned versus overlap finding, the two recitations really did pull against each other: if the openings are structurally aligned with the passages before the lid moves, the registered position adds nothing. 'Positioned to align with' keeps the module element describing where the openings sit on the frame while leaving the actual alignment to be produced by the indexing rib, which is the feature claim 1 rests on. This is a wording change only and narrows nothing.

The unhatched cassette blocks were a self-contradiction inside one brief: the plane was stated to cut them while they were specified plain. They are hatched now, consistent with every other cut body in that view, and the schematic rectangular outline convention is unchanged and still confined to the brief.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md still lists no references, so there is nothing to cite, nothing to distinguish and no reference vocabulary to avoid. The Background carries no citation and states the problem in the inventor's own terms: the temperature spread that results when a refrigerant mass is laid against a payload, the dependence of any imposed circulation path on an alignment the packer must produce by hand, the condensate left by repeated opening of a reusable carrier, and the erasure of an excursion once the refrigerant recovers. Each of those states the technical problem that a specific claimed feature solves, and the solution appears in the Detailed Description in the same words the claims use. The distinguishing weight remains on lid-driven registration: the closing travel of the lid shifting the thermal module until the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so the alignment that the passive circulation path depends on is produced by an act the packer cannot skip. This turn's claim edit strengthens that position rather than weakening it, because the module element no longer recites the openings as already aligned and the registration step now carries the alignment on its own. The secondary positions are unchanged: the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator that reports the state of the refrigerant itself and survives its recovery, and the wick in a condensate channel serviced by a pull tab without opening or removing a cassette. Because no search was run, none of this has been measured against real references, and a search should be run before filing.

Claims 1 and 13 and the corresponding description sentence now recite the peripheral outlet openings as positioned to align with the side supply passages, so the registration limitation is no longer pre-empted, and the two upright blocks that FIG. 1's plane cuts are hatched. The numeral table is unchanged, every numeral still appears on a sheet, and no drawing detail was promoted into the application text.

reasoning: The overlap finding was a geometry error I introduced last turn when I made the FIG. 5 region adjoin the FIG. 4 region on the same side. For the indicator detail I deleted the cassette block rather than reconciling the geometry, because the disclosure says only that the stem is thermally coupled to one cassette and gives no coupling geometry. Drawing the cassette in open space against the shell wall was the figure inventing a path that would have had to cross the side supply passage, contradicting the claim that the indicator does not throttle those passages. The thermal coupling stays where the disclosure puts it, in the description.

The section-line finding needed a source view, and I gave FIG. 6 its own rather than adding the indicator and a cutting line to FIG. 1. FIG. 1 already carries the maximum eight numerals and sits within a few characters of the brief length ceiling, so the additions would have forced disclosed geometry off that sheet, which is exactly what the figure-plan rule forbids. reasoning: The previous wording said only that 'the same designation is repeated at both ends'. I had phrased it that way to keep a bare digit out of the brief, but it left the arrows described collectively and never wrote the designation itself, so the section-line check could not find either element. The fix is to say both explicitly.

I wrote the two ends as separate sentences, each naming its own arrow, its direction, and the designation beside it, so the brief affirmatively contains an arrow and a designation for each end rather than a single collective statement that has to be read as covering both.

The digit is always written as 'the section designation 7' or inside 'line 7-7', never as a bare number next to a part name, so it reads as drawing annotation rather than a reference numeral. It stays out of numerals.md and out of the reference-numeral list, where a section designation does not belong.

Nothing else moved. The check named only the FIG. 6 source-view brief, and the enlargement curves designated FIG. 3, FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 on FIG. 1 are not sectional views, so they need no arrows and were left alone. A proportion conveys technical substance and is expressly outside the generic-outline depiction convention, even though the slab shape itself is properly tagged "shown schematically".
29	  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-2.md, delete the proportion: replace "each parallel to the long side walls and running most of the frame length" with "each parallel to the long side walls, their extent along the frame shown schematically".

No change to the description or claims is needed; both remain generic ("a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position").
31	  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-7.md, replace that sentence with "A spring, shown schematically as a coil of aligned loops within the outline and drawn extended, acts on the shaft in the direction of its outward projection. This spring is the spring 86."

The exposed position is fully inventor-supported, so the cure is a text statement, not a figure change.
33	  - Suggested fix: In draft/07-drawings.md, append ", the indicator stem being shown in the exposed position" to the FIG. 6 entry (after "the outer end of the indicator stem") and to the FIG. 7 entry (after "the temperature-responsive latch and the spring"). In draft/08-detailed-description.md, after "The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44.", add "FIG. 6 and FIG. 7 show the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position."

36	the wording or figure specification unambiguous enough that the check passes.

Perspective view of the thermal module alone, seen from above and in front so that the open top, the near long side and the near short end are visible. Plain black line work on white, no hatching. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

The main body is a rectangular open frame, shown schematically. It has a near long side wall, a far long side wall, a left short end wall, a right short end wall and a bottom panel joining them. The top is open. This frame is the spacer frame 42; the spacer frame 42 together with the two slabs it holds is the thermal module 40.

Two flat rectangular slabs stand upright inside the frame, each parallel to the long side walls and running most of the frame length. They are spaced apart across the depth of the frame, leaving an open central gap between their confronting broad faces, and each is also spaced from the adjacent long side wall, leaving an open vertical channel between slab and wall. The top edge of the near long side wall carries an upwardly open groove at mid-length, running across the thickness of that wall. This groove is the mating channel 56.

In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.

The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12.

The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. The tray side walls 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.

The thermal module

Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 before packing.

The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, each guide duct 50 located beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 positioned to align with the side supply passages 28.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and the registration is completed by the closing of the lid. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is therefore created by an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 of the outer shell 10 lie beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. The resilient feet 58 maintain a downward holding force during transport, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.

The circulation path

In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Air warmed in the product region rises to the central inlet opening 48, and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes descends through the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, so that circulation proceeds without any powered air mover.

Condensate management

A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough extending around the product tray 20. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the condensate channel 70 and the absorbent wick 72 remain in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed. Discharge openings 76 are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

Mechanical exposure indicator

The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. FIG. 6 shows the mechanical exposure indicator 80 as it appears from outside the outer shell 10, at the outer surface of a side wall 14. Referring to FIG. 7, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.

Operation

In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. Goods are placed in the product tray 20 and the product tray 20 is placed in the outer shell 10 so that the tray feet 22 stand on the floor 12, leaving the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20 and the two side supply passages 28 between the tray side walls 26 and the side walls 14. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20. The insulated lid 60 is then closed, whereby the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 and shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position, the resilient feet 58 are pressed against the ledges 18 to retain the thermal module 40, and the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. Air thereafter circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover. At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.

Essential and optional features

Two phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42, opposed across the central space. Entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.

The described implementations are examples. A person skilled in the art may combine, substitute or omit the described features within the scope of the claims that follow.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is nothing to cite, nothing to distinguish and no reference vocabulary to avoid. The Background carries no citation and states the problem in the inventor's own terms: the temperature spread that results when a refrigerant mass is laid against a payload, the dependence of any imposed circulation path on an alignment the packer must produce by hand, the condensate left by repeated opening of a reusable carrier, and the erasure of an excursion once the refrigerant recovers. Each states the technical problem that a specific claimed feature solves, and the solution appears in the Detailed Description in the same words the claims use, which is what a later argument would be built from. The distinguishing weight remains on lid-driven registration: the closing travel of the lid shifting the thermal module until the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so the alignment the passive circulation path depends on is produced by an act the packer cannot skip. The secondary positions are the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator, which reports the state of the refrigerant itself and survives its recovery, and the wick in a condensate channel serviced by a pull tab without opening or removing a cassette. This turn changed only figure briefs and two short text clauses, so no claim scope moved. Because no search was run, none of this has been measured against real references, and a search should be run before filing.

Title, "Not applicable" cross-reference, and "Not applicable" government-support statement match input/brief.md (no priority claim, no federally sponsored research). No means-plus-function language; three statutory classes; abstract is one paragraph of about 140 words. Background is prior-art characterization only. No drafting notes, placeholders, open questions, or unresolved alternatives remain in draft/ or figures/ (grep for TODO/TBD/FIXME/comment markers is clean there). (1) Section-line direction: FIG-6.md specifies a horizontal cutting-plane line with both arrows pointing toward the bottom of the sheet, which defines a horizontal cutting plane viewed downward, but FIG-7.md describes a vertical section ("upright wall body", latch "above the shaft ... projecting downward with its lower end adjacent the upper surface of the shaft"). The 7-7 designation itself is repeated correctly at both ends and is consistent across draft/07-drawings.md, FIG-6.md and FIG-7.md; only the plane and view direction are wrong. (2) Ledge/outlet vertical ordering: FIG-3.md ends the sectioned spacer frame "down to the level of the ledge 18" with the resilient foot at the frame's "lower left corner", while FIG-1.md assigns the outboard channel opening to the lower-left (FIG. 4) region and FIG-4.md draws the side wall's inner surface as "flat vertical ... straight from the top of the fragment to the bottom", i.e. the peripheral outlet opening 54 lies below the ledge - which the frame cannot reach if it terminates at the ledge. 14	- **[major] Cutting-plane line 7-7 in FIG. 6 defines a horizontal section viewed downward, but FIG. 7 is drawn as a vertical section** (figures/FIG-6.md line 11 (and its section-designation bullet, line 14) versus figures/FIG-7.md lines 3-13; draft/07-draw) - FIG-6.md places the section line as "A horizontal broken line [that] crosses the fragment at the level of the smaller outline", with a short arrow at each end "pointing toward the bottom of the drawing area". In an elevation of the outer wall surface, a horizontal cutting-plane line with arrows pointing down specifies a horizontal cutting plane seen from above. FIG-7.md, however, describes a vertical section: the wall appears as "A thick hatched upright wall body", and the latch is "A small block [that] sits above the shaft within the outline, to the right of the coil spring, projecting downward with its lower end adjacent the upper surface of the shaft". Real-world vertical relationships such as "above the shaft", "projecting downward" and "the upper surface of the shaft" cannot appear in a plan section taken at stem level; a latch above that plane would lie outside the cut. The resulting view and the source-view brief therefore disagree about the plane and the direction of sight even though the 7-7 designation itself is repeated correctly at both ends of the line and is used identically in draft/07-drawings.md ("carrying the line 7-7 on which FIG. 7 is taken" and "taken on line 7-7 of FIG. 6"). This broken line is the cutting-plane line for the sectional view FIG. 7. Its upper end carries a short arrow pointing toward the left side of the drawing area and, beside that arrow, the section designation 7. Its lower end carries a second short arrow, also pointing toward the left side of the drawing area, and beside that arrow the section designation 7 is repeated. # FIG. 1

Schematic vertical section of an assembled passive cold-chain carrier, on a plane cutting both upright blocks in the module body and the groove in its top. Plain black line work on white, hatching on cut material, all inside the drawing area.

Two thick hatched upright wall bodies and a thick hatched bottom body joining them form a container open at the top: the sectioned outer shell 10, its bottom body the floor 12. Below its top end each wall body carries an inward-projecting block. A thick hatched slab across both top ends is the insulated lid 60, closed, a narrow rib projecting down from its underside inboard of the left top end and a small compressible body between it and each top end.

Within it, a sectioned open-top box with thin hatched walls and a bottom wall is the product tray 20, standing above the floor 12 on short hatched blocks, two appearing in this section, shown schematically, the tray feet 22; the space beneath the bottom wall is the lower return passage 24. Its walls stand clear of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap each side, stop short of the floor 12, and carry small openings below bottom wall level. A shallow trough at the foot of each gap holds an elongated absorbent body, a narrow strip rising from the right-hand body into the gap.

Above the tray and below the lid 60 is an elongated hatched body in section, the thermal module 40, open downward at its centre, holding two upright hatched rectangular blocks, shown schematically, spaced apart. An open vertical channel runs down outboard of each block, opening through the body's outboard side above the gap and through its downward lower end over the trough. A small block is flattened between the body underside and each inward-projecting block. A groove opening upward in the top surface takes the lower end of the rib.

Three broken-line curves are drawn: one upper left around the rib, groove, left wall top, the compressible body on that top end, the left projecting block and the small block on it; one lower left around the left outboard channel opening, left gap, tray openings, tray bottom wall and the space beneath it; one lower right around the right channel lower end, its downward opening, the right trough, absorbent body and the strip rising from it.

- FIG. 3: outside the upper left curve.
- FIG. 4: outside the lower left curve.
- FIG. 5: outside the lower right curve.

- 10: outside the container, lead to the shell.
- 12: well inside the bottom body.
- 20: well inside the left tray wall.
- 22: well inside one short block under the tray.
- 24: inside the space under the tray bottom wall.
- 40: outside the container, lead to the module.
- 60: well inside the top slab.
- 100: outside the container, lead to the carrier.

All three findings are fixed.

- **Cutting-plane direction** — `figures/FIG-6.md` now carries a vertical broken cutting-plane line through the indicator outline, from a short distance above the fragment's upper edge to a short distance below its lower edge, with a short arrow at the upper end pointing toward the left side of the drawing area and the section designation 7 beside it, a second arrow at the lower end pointing the same way with the designation 7 repeated, and the statement that both arrows give the direction in which FIG. 7 is seen so the line reads line 7-7. FIG. 7 and the Brief Description needed no change.
- **Ledge above outlet** — one ordering is now stated in all three briefs. FIG. 3 carries the sectioned spacer frame downward past the lower edge of the fragment, shown cut off there, and places the resilient foot at the level of ledge 18 between a downwardly facing outboard surface of the frame and the ledge top. - **Lower right curve contents** — that curve now encloses the right channel lower end and downward opening, the right tray wall lower part with its openings, the right gap, the bottom body there, the right trough, the absorbent body and the strip, matching everything FIG. 5 draws.

FIG. 1 had to be compressed again to hold the added geometry within the brief length limit. Numeral 24 moved off that sheet, where the space beneath the tray is now shown as open space without a label; the lower return passage 24 stays labelled on FIG. 4, which is the view the Brief Description says shows it, so every numeral still appears on a sheet and nothing was removed from the numeral table or the text.

input.summary: All three findings are fixed. The cutting-plane line on FIG. 6 is now vertical, with an arrow at each end pointing toward the left side of the drawing area and the section designation 7 repeated at both ends, which matches the vertical section FIG. 7 draws with the outer surface at the left. The ledge and the peripheral outlet opening now have one consistent vertical ordering across FIG. 1, FIG. 3 and FIG. 4: the resilient foot sits at ledge level against a downwardly facing outboard surface of the spacer frame, the frame continues downward past the lower edge of the FIG. 3 fragment, the outboard channel opening lies below the projecting block and above the gap, and the FIG. 4 fragment is taken below the level of the inward projections. The lower right broken-line curve on FIG. 1 now encloses everything FIG. 5 draws, including the right tray wall lower part with its openings, the right gap and the adjoining bottom body. FIG. 1 was compressed again to stay within the brief length limit; numeral 24 moved off that sheet and remains labelled on FIG. 4, so every numeral still appears on a drawing and nothing left the numeral table or the application text.
reasoning: The section-line finding was a geometry error, not a labelling one. FIG. 7 shows an upright wall body with the latch above the shaft, which only exists in a vertical cut, so a horizontal cutting line viewed downward described a different view from the one drawn. Turning the line vertical and the arrows toward the left of the sheet makes the source view produce exactly the section FIG. 7 shows, with the shell outside on the left and the inside on the right, and leaves the 7-7 designation chain untouched in FIG. 7 and the Brief Description.

The ledge/outlet conflict came from FIG. 3 terminating the spacer frame at ledge level while FIG. 1 and FIG. 4 needed the outlet opening on the frame's outboard face below that level. I resolved it by letting the frame run past the bottom of the FIG. 3 fragment and by giving the resilient foot a downwardly facing outboard surface of the frame to press on, which keeps the disclosed relationship, the feet pressed against the shell ledges, while leaving the frame free to continue down to where the outlet opening meets the side supply passage. Both relationships are inventor-supported; only their relative levels were inconsistent, and no structure was added.

FIG. 4 states its fragment is taken below the level of the inward projections rather than saying no projection appears there. A positive statement of where the fragment sits does the same work as the negative one and does not reintroduce the kind of generic linework ban that failed an earlier gate.

The lower right curve list was cured on the parent view by widening the region, not by trimming FIG. 5, since the tray wall openings, the gap and the bottom body are all disclosed structure that FIG. 5 legitimately shows.

FIG. 1 has been at the brief length ceiling for several rounds and this turn added the ledge ordering and the longer curve list, so something had to give. I moved numeral 24 to FIG. 4 rather than dropping any geometry: the space beneath the tray is still drawn on FIG. 1 as open space and is still enclosed by the lower left curve, the lower return passage 24 is labelled on FIG. 4, which is the view the Brief Description says shows it, and neither the description nor the FIG. 1 entry claims that numeral appears on FIG. 1. That is label redistribution, not deletion.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is nothing to cite, nothing to distinguish and no reference vocabulary to avoid. The Background carries no citation and states the problem in the inventor's own terms: the temperature spread that results when a refrigerant mass is laid against a payload, the dependence of any imposed circulation path on an alignment the packer must produce by hand, the condensate left by repeated opening of a reusable carrier, and the erasure of an excursion once the refrigerant recovers. Each states the technical problem that a specific claimed feature solves, and the solution appears in the Detailed Description in the same words the claims use. The distinguishing weight remains on lid-driven registration: the closing travel of the lid shifting the thermal module until the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so the alignment the passive circulation path depends on is produced by an act the packer cannot skip. The secondary positions are the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator, which reports the state of the refrigerant itself and survives its recovery, and the wick in a condensate channel serviced by a pull tab without opening or removing a cassette. This turn changed only figure briefs, so no claim scope moved. Because no search was run, none of this has been measured against real references, and a search should be run before filing.

In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.

The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12.

The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. The tray side walls 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.

The thermal module

Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 before packing.

The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, each guide duct 50 located beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 positioned to align with the side supply passages 28.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and the registration is completed by the closing of the lid. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is therefore created by an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 of the outer shell 10 lie beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. The resilient feet 58 maintain a downward holding force during transport, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.

The circulation path

In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Air warmed in the product region rises to the central inlet opening 48, and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes descends through the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, so that circulation proceeds without any powered air mover.

Condensate management

A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough extending around the product tray 20. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the condensate channel 70 and the absorbent wick 72 remain in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed. Discharge openings 76 are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

Mechanical exposure indicator

The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. FIG. 6 shows the mechanical exposure indicator 80 as it appears from outside the outer shell 10, at the outer surface of a side wall 14. Referring to FIG. 7, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44. FIG. 6 and FIG. 7 show the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.

Operation

In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. Goods are placed in the product tray 20 and the product tray 20 is placed in the outer shell 10 so that the tray feet 22 stand on the floor 12, leaving the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20 and the two side supply passages 28 between the tray side walls 26 and the side walls 14. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20. The insulated lid 60 is then closed, whereby the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 and shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position, the resilient feet 58 are pressed against the ledges 18 to retain the thermal module 40, and the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. Air thereafter circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover. At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.

Essential and optional features

Two phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42, opposed across the central space. Entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.

The described implementations are examples. A person skilled in the art may combine, substitute or omit the described features within the scope of the claims that follow.

In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Air warmed in the product region rises to the central inlet opening 48, and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes descends through the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, so that circulation proceeds without any powered air mover.

The detailed description's circulation paragraph now ends at the lower return passage, matching claim 1, claim 17, the Summary and the Abstract, and the clause asserting that air rises again from that passage into the product region is gone. No opening was added to the tray bottom wall, so the FIG. 1 and FIG. 4 briefs are untouched. Claims 16 and 19 now characterise the condensate channel the way claim 6 and the description do, as extending around the product tray within the outer shell, so one element is described one way across the whole claim set. Claim 6 and the description are unchanged. In claim 19 the pull tab phrase was moved next to the drawing step so it cannot be read as modifying the channel; the step covers the same act. reasoning: The return-leg clause was the description asserting a closure the inventor never wrote and the drawings cannot show. The disclosed path ends at the lower return passage, and the only openings in the tray are the perforations in the side wall below the bottom wall, so nothing depicted connects that passage to the tray interior. Deleting the clause was the correct cure rather than adding bottom-wall openings, because openings there would be structure with no source passage behind it, invented to rescue a sentence.

That also aligns the description with the claims. Claim 1 and claim 17 already stopped at the return passage, so the description was claiming a leg broader than the claims recite, which is the wrong direction for support: the description must carry the claims, not exceed the disclosure.

The paragraph immediately after was left alone deliberately. It says warm air in the product region rises to the central inlet and cooled air descends through the ducts and passages, both of which are express disclosure sentences, and it explains why the circulation needs no powered air mover without asserting the undisclosed closure.

On the condensate channel, the inventor located it relative to the tray, and claim 6 and the description both follow that. Claims 16 and 19 had made it a feature of the shell, which is a different structural relationship for the same element. Saying it extends around the product tray within the outer shell keeps both facts the source supports, its position around the tray and its staying behind in the shell when the tray is lifted out, and makes the three claims use one characterisation.

The reorder in claim 19 is readability, not scope. As drafted, 'out of a condensate channel ... by a pull tab' let the pull tab phrase attach to the channel rather than to the drawing step. Putting it directly after the verb removes the ambiguity without changing what the step requires.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is nothing to cite, nothing to distinguish and no reference vocabulary to avoid. The Background carries no citation and states the problem in the inventor's own terms: the temperature spread that results when a refrigerant mass is laid against a payload, the dependence of any imposed circulation path on an alignment the packer must produce by hand, the condensate left by repeated opening of a reusable carrier, and the erasure of an excursion once the refrigerant recovers. Each states the technical problem that a specific claimed feature solves, and the solution appears in the Detailed Description in the same words the claims use, which is what a later argument would be built from. The distinguishing weight remains on lid-driven registration: the closing travel of the lid shifting the thermal module until the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so the alignment the passive circulation path depends on is produced by an act the packer cannot skip. The secondary positions are the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator, which reports the state of the refrigerant itself and survives its recovery, and the wick in a condensate channel serviced by a pull tab without opening or removing a cassette. This turn removed an unsupported sentence clause and conformed two dependent claims to the description, so no independent claim scope moved. Because no search was run, none of this has been measured against real references, and a search should be run before filing.

In claim 19 the pull tab phrase now follows the drawing step so it cannot be read as modifying the channel, with no change to what the step requires. The numeral table, the Brief Description and all seven figure briefs are unchanged, and every figure brief remains within the length limit.

structured_output.summary: Both findings are fixed in the text. The detailed description's circulation paragraph now ends at the lower return passage, matching claim 1, claim 17, the Summary and the Abstract, and the clause asserting that air rises again from that passage into the product region is gone. No opening was added to the tray bottom wall, so the FIG. 1 and FIG. 4 briefs are untouched. Claims 16 and 19 now characterise the condensate channel the way claim 6 and the description do, as extending around the product tray within the outer shell, so one element is described one way across the whole claim set. Claim 6 and the description are unchanged. In claim 19 the pull tab phrase was moved next to the drawing step so it cannot be read as modifying the channel; the step covers the same act. The numeral table, the Brief Description and all seven figure briefs are unchanged and every brief remains within the length limit.
reasoning: The return-leg clause was the description asserting a closure the inventor never wrote and the drawings cannot show. The disclosed path ends at the lower return passage, and the only openings in the tray are the perforations in the side wall below the bottom wall, so nothing depicted connects that passage to the tray interior. Deleting the clause was the correct cure rather than adding bottom-wall openings, because openings there would be structure with no source passage behind it, invented to rescue a sentence.

That also aligns the description with the claims. Claim 1 and claim 17 already stopped at the return passage, so the description was claiming a leg broader than the claims recite, which is the wrong direction for support: the description must carry the claims, not exceed the disclosure.

The paragraph immediately after was left alone deliberately. It says warm air in the product region rises to the central inlet and cooled air descends through the ducts and passages, both of which are express disclosure sentences, and it explains why the circulation needs no powered air mover without asserting the undisclosed closure.

On the condensate channel, the inventor located it relative to the tray, and claim 6 and the description both follow that. Claims 16 and 19 had made it a feature of the shell, which is a different structural relationship for the same element. Saying it extends around the product tray within the outer shell keeps both facts the source supports, its position around the tray and its staying behind in the shell when the tray is lifted out, and makes the three claims use one characterisation.

The reorder in claim 19 is readability, not scope. As drafted, 'out of a condensate channel ... by a pull tab' let the pull tab phrase attach to the channel rather than to the drawing step. Putting it directly after the verb removes the ambiguity without changing what the step requires.
