A passive cold-chain carrier is disclosed in which the closing of the lid, rather than the care of the packer, establishes the circulation path.

In one aspect, the carrier includes an insulated outer shell having a floor and side walls, a product tray removably received in the outer shell, a thermal module removably received in the outer shell above the product tray, and an insulated lid. The product tray is supported above the floor by tray feet so that a lower return passage remains between the product tray and the floor, and the tray side walls are spaced inward from the side walls of the outer shell to form two side supply passages. The thermal module includes a rigid spacer frame and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame, the spacer frame defining a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings. The insulated lid carries a depending indexing rib positioned to enter a mating channel of the spacer frame as the lid closes and to shift the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages.

In the registered position the shell, the product tray, the thermal module and the lid cooperate to define a circulation path along which air rising from a product region within the product tray enters the central inlet opening, divides along faces of the two phase-change cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage. The carrier is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover.

The technical effect of lid-driven registration is that the alignment on which the circulation path depends is created by an act the packer cannot omit. The thermal module is placed in the outer shell above the product tray, and the depending indexing rib entering the mating channel shifts the module into the position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages. The seal made by a compressible lid gasket against the upper edge of the outer shell occurs after registration, so the carrier is not closed against a module that is still out of position. The same closing movement presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the outer shell, so that the registered module is held down against the product tray and cannot lift away from it under the vibration and inversion of transport.

In a further aspect, a shallow condensate channel extends around the product tray and receives a removable absorbent wick. Discharge openings at lower ends of the guide ducts deliver condensate into the condensate channel. A pull tab on the absorbent wick remains accessible when the product tray is removed, so the wick is replaced without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service.

In a further aspect, the outer shell carries a mechanical exposure indicator visible from outside the carrier. An indicator stem is thermally coupled to one of the phase-change cassettes and is retained by a temperature-responsive latch. If that cassette softens enough to release the latch, a spring moves the indicator stem to a latched exposed position, and the indication remains exposed after the cassette cools again, being reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The indicator therefore reports the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends, survives recovery of the cassette, and requires no battery. The exposure indicator does not control airflow, so the circulation path is unaffected by whether the indicator has tripped.

In a further aspect, a method includes fitting conditioned phase-change cassettes to the spacer frame, placing product in the product tray, placing the product tray in the outer shell, placing the thermal module above the product tray, and closing the insulated lid so that the depending indexing rib enters the mating channel and shifts the thermal module into the registered position, whereafter air circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover.

The features summarised above may be used together or separately, and the summary is not a statement of the scope of the claims.

# FIG. 1

Schematic vertical section of an assembled cold-chain carrier, on a plane cutting both upright blocks in the module body and the groove in its top. Plain black line work, hatching on cut material, all inside the drawing area.

Two thick hatched upright wall bodies joined by a thick hatched bottom body form a container open at top: the sectioned outer shell 10, its bottom body the floor 12. Below its top end each wall body carries an inward-projecting block. A thick hatched slab across both top ends is the insulated lid 60, closed, a narrow rib projecting down from its underside inboard of the left top end, a small compressible body between slab and each top end.

Within it, a sectioned open-top box with thin hatched walls and a bottom wall is the product tray 20, standing above the floor 12 on short hatched blocks, two appearing in this section, shown schematically, the tray feet 22, with open space beneath. Its walls stand clear of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap each side, stop short of the floor 12, and carry small openings below bottom wall. A shallow trough at each gap foot holds an elongated absorbent body, a narrow strip rising from the right-hand one into the gap.

Above the tray, below the lid 60, is an elongated hatched body in section, the thermal module 40, open downward at its centre, holding two upright hatched rectangular blocks, shown schematically, spaced apart. An open vertical channel runs down outboard of each block, opening through the body's outboard side below the projecting block and above the gap, and through its downward lower end over the trough. A small block is flattened between a down-facing outboard surface of the body and each inward-projecting block, the body continuing down inboard of it. A groove opening upward in the top surface takes the lower end of the rib.

Three broken-line curves are drawn: one upper left around the rib, groove, left wall top, the compressible body there, the left projecting block and the small block on it; one lower left around the left outboard channel opening, left gap, tray openings, tray bottom wall and the space under it; one lower right around the right channel lower end and downward opening, the right tray wall lower part with its openings, the right gap, the bottom body there, the right trough, absorbent body and strip.

- FIG. 3: outside the upper left curve.
- FIG. 4: outside the lower left curve.
- FIG. 5: outside the lower right curve.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 10: outside the container, to the shell.
- 12: well inside the bottom body.
- 20: well inside the left tray wall.
- 22: well inside a short block under the tray.
- 40: outside the container, to the module.
- 60: well inside the top slab.
- 100: outside the container, to the carrier.

# FIG. 1

Schematic vertical section of an assembled cold-chain carrier, on a plane cutting both upright blocks in the module body and the groove in its top. Plain black line work, hatching on cut material, all inside the drawing area.

Two thick hatched upright wall bodies joined by a thick hatched bottom body form a container open at top: the sectioned outer shell 10, its bottom body the floor 12. Below its top end each wall body carries an inward-projecting block. A thick hatched slab across both top ends is the insulated lid 60, closed, a narrow rib projecting down from its underside inboard of the left top end, a small compressible body between slab and each top end.

Within it, a sectioned open-top box with thin hatched walls and a bottom wall is the product tray 20, standing above the floor 12 on short hatched blocks, two appearing here, shown schematically, the tray feet 22, with open space beneath. Its walls stand clear of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap each side, stop short of the floor 12, and carry small openings below bottom wall. One shallow trough runs around the tray and is cut at both gap feet, appearing at each, and one elongated absorbent body lying in it appears in both, a narrow strip rising from the right-hand appearance into the gap.

Above the tray, below the lid 60, is an elongated hatched body in section, the thermal module 40, open downward at its centre, holding two upright hatched rectangular blocks, shown schematically, spaced apart. An open vertical channel runs down outboard of each block, opening through the body's outboard side below the projecting block and above the gap, and through its downward lower end over the trough. A small block is flattened between a down-facing outboard surface of the body and each inward-projecting block, the body continuing down inboard of it. A groove opening upward in the top surface takes the lower end of the rib.

Three broken-line curves are drawn: one upper left around the rib, groove, left wall top, compressible body, left projecting block and the small block on it; one lower left around the left outboard channel opening, left gap, tray openings, tray bottom wall and space under it; one lower right around the right channel lower end and downward opening, the right tray wall lower part with its openings, the right gap, bottom body, right trough, absorbent body and strip.

- FIG. 3: outside the upper left curve.
- FIG. 4: outside the lower left curve.
- FIG. 5: outside the lower right curve.

- 10: outside the container, to the shell.
- 12: well inside the bottom body.
- 20: well inside the left tray wall.
- 22: well inside a short block under the tray.
- 40: outside the container, to the module.
- 60: well inside the top slab.
- 100: outside the container, to the carrier.

content.text:
Both findings are fixed.

- **Unsupported transport conditions** — `draft/06-summary.md` now reads "so that the registered module is held down against the product tray and cannot lift away from it during transport." Vibration and inversion are gone; that was the only place either word appeared, and the Summary now matches the Detailed Description sentence and the disclosure's own wording. The directional convention in the Detailed Description, which fixes the carrier in its normal upright orientation, is no longer contradicted.
- **Single condensate channel and wick in FIG. 1** — the trough sentence now reads "One shallow trough runs around the tray, cut at both gap feet so it appears at each, and one elongated absorbent body in it appears in both, a narrow strip rising from the right-hand appearance into the gap." That states one channel and one wick sectioned twice, which is what claim 6 and the description recite, and the strip still rises from only one appearance. The numeral list is unchanged, and 70, 72 and 74 remain labelled on FIG. 5.

To fit that longer sentence within the brief length limit I tightened wording elsewhere in the same brief. No geometry, contact, opening, curve content or numeral was dropped. No other file changed: claims, numeral table, Brief Description and the other six briefs are untouched.

input.summary: Both findings are fixed. The Summary sentence about retention now ends "cannot lift away from it during transport", removing the vibration and inversion conditions that no source passage affirms and that sat badly with the application's own upright-orientation convention and buoyancy-driven loop. The FIG. 1 brief now states that one shallow trough runs around the tray and is cut at both gap feet so it appears at each, and that one elongated absorbent body lying in it appears in both, with the narrow strip rising from the right-hand appearance, so the brief no longer reads as two channels each with its own wick. Surrounding wording in the same brief was tightened so the longer sentence stays within the brief length limit, with no geometry, contact, opening, curve content or numeral lost. Nothing else changed: the claims, the numeral table, the Brief Description and the other six figure briefs are untouched.
reasoning: The Summary was asserting operating conditions the inventor never gave. The disclosure says only that the module cannot lift away from the tray during transport, so I cut back to exactly that. Inversion was the worse of the two: it is an affirmative statement about how the carrier is handled, and the rest of the application defines its directional terms by the carrier standing upright with the lid uppermost and relies on warm air rising and cooled air descending. Keeping it would have left the document arguing with itself.

The retention effect itself is untouched. The resilient feet still press against the ledges under the closing movement and still hold the registered module down against the tray, which is the disclosed function and what claims 2, 14 and 18 recite. Only the invented environment around it is gone.

The FIG. 1 trough wording was a count problem, not a geometry problem. The section plane genuinely cuts the surrounding channel at both side gaps, so two troughs and two pieces of wick appear in the view, but the previous phrasing specified a trough with its own absorbent body at each gap, which asserts two of each. Saying one channel and one wick, cut so that each appears twice, describes the same picture without contradicting claim 6 and the description.
The pull tab strip stays on one appearance only, which is what a single continuous wick with one tab requires, and I left it there rather than mirroring it to the other side.

FIG. 1 has been at its length ceiling for several rounds, so the longer sentence had to be paid for. I took it out of redundancy in the same brief, for example dropping an article, a repeated part name and the word rectangular from a block that is already marked shown schematically, rather than out of any body, contact, opening, curve content or numeral.

figures/FIG-1.md: 'A shallow trough at each gap foot holds an elongated absorbent body, a narrow strip rising from the right-hand one into the gap.' becomes 'One shallow trough runs around the tray, cut at both gap feet so it appears at each, and one elongated absorbent body in it appears in both, a narrow strip rising from the right-hand appearance into the gap.'

figures/FIG-1.md: wording tightened elsewhere in the brief to stay within the length limit, including 'two appearing here' for the tray feet, dropping 'rectangular' from the schematic module blocks, and trimming articles in the lid, module and curve-content sentences. All bodies, contacts, openings, curve contents and numerals are unchanged.
input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is nothing to cite, nothing to distinguish and no reference vocabulary to avoid. The Background carries no citation and states the problem in the inventor's own terms: the temperature spread that results when a refrigerant mass is laid against a payload, the dependence of any imposed circulation path on an alignment the packer must produce by hand, the condensate left by repeated opening of a reusable carrier, and the erasure of an excursion once the refrigerant recovers. Each states the technical problem that a specific claimed feature solves, and the solution appears in the Detailed Description in the same words the claims use, which is what a later argument would be built from. The distinguishing weight remains on lid-driven registration: the closing travel of the lid shifting the thermal module until the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so the alignment the passive circulation path depends on is produced by an act the packer cannot skip. The secondary positions are the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator, which reports the state of the refrigerant itself and survives its recovery, and the wick in a condensate channel serviced by a pull tab without opening or removing a cassette. This turn removed an unsupported clause from the Summary and clarified one figure brief, so no claim scope moved. Because no search was run, none of this has been measured against real references, and a search should be run before filing.
input.answer: Both items are fixed. The Summary now says the registered module is held down against the product tray and cannot lift away from it during transport, which is the inventor's own statement; vibration and inversion appeared nowhere else in the application and are gone. The retention mechanism itself, the resilient feet pressed against the ledges by the closing movement, is unchanged. In the FIG. 1 brief, the condensate structure now reads as one shallow trough running around the tray, cut at both gap feet so it appears at each, with one elongated absorbent body in it appearing in both and the narrow strip rising from the right-hand appearance. That matches the single channel and single wick recited in claim 6 and in the description, and numerals 70, 72 and 74 remain on FIG. 5. Fitting the longer sentence required tightening wording elsewhere in the same brief; no geometry, contact, opening, curve content or numeral was dropped. The claims, the numeral table, the Brief Description and the other six figure briefs are untouched.

The top edge of the near long side wall carries an upwardly open groove at mid-length, running across the thickness of that wall. This groove is the mating channel 56.

Small blocks project downward from the underside of the frame, two visible at the front, shown schematically. These blocks are the resilient feet 58.

content.text:
Both findings are fixed inside `figures/FIG-2.md`.

- **Guide ducts open at the bottom** — the bottom panel now carries, besides the central inlet opening 48, a further through opening at the foot of the channel beside each slab, so the viewer looks down through the panel there and each channel is open at its lower end. That matches FIG. 1, where the channel opens through its downward lower end over the trough, and FIG. 5, where the discharge opening 76 passes through the downwardly facing bottom surface, and it restores the condensate route the description and claims 7 and 16 recite. The openings are described generically on this sheet rather than labelled 76, which keeps FIG. 2 at eight numerals and leaves 76 labelled on FIG. 5, the view that enlarges it.
- **Resilient feet on an outboard step** — the lower part of each long side wall now carries an outward step, shown schematically, whose downwardly facing surface lies above the bottom panel level and outboard of it, with the small blocks projecting down from that surface. That is the geometry FIG. 1 and FIG. 3 require, a foot on a downwardly facing outboard surface with frame material continuing below and inboard of it, and it is consistent with FIG. 4 showing module material below ledge level. The leader for 58 now points into a block below that step.

Fitting both changes within the brief length limit meant tightening wording elsewhere in the same brief; the frame, slabs, central gap, channels, outlet openings, groove and every numeral are unchanged. I also dropped "at mid-length" from the groove description, an exact placement the disclosure does not give. No file outside `figures/FIG-2.md` changed.

input.summary: Both findings are fixed, and both fixes stayed inside figures/FIG-2.md. The spacer frame's bottom panel now carries a further through opening at the foot of the channel beside each slab, so each guide duct is open at its lower end as FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 already showed, and the condensate route recited in the description and in claims 7 and 16 is no longer contradicted. The resilient feet now project downward from an outward step on the lower part of each long side wall, whose downwardly facing surface lies above the bottom panel level and outboard of it, which is the geometry FIG. 1 and FIG. 3 require and which leaves frame material below and inboard of each foot as FIG. 4 shows. The two new bottom-panel openings are described generically rather than numbered, so the sheet stays at eight numerals and numeral 76 remains on FIG. 5. Wording elsewhere in the same brief was tightened to hold both changes within the brief length limit, and no other file changed.
reasoning: Both defects were FIG. 2 disagreeing with the rest of the set about the same numbered parts, so I corrected FIG. 2 rather than the three briefs that already matched each other and the claims. The discharge openings at the lower ends of the guide ducts and the resilient feet pressed against the shell ledges are both disclosed, so nothing new entered the drawings.

I depicted the two bottom-panel openings without labelling them 76. Adding that numeral would have made nine on the sheet, over the per-sheet limit, and would have forced another numeral off a view where it does useful work. The openings are still drawn, the geometry conflict is cured, and 76 stays labelled on FIG. 5, the view that enlarges the duct lower end.

For the same reason I left the FIG. 2 entry in the Brief Description alone. It lists parts that are labelled on that sheet, and adding a discharge opening to that list would have obliged the brief to number one.

input.summary: The one finding is fixed. In figures/FIG-1.md the leader for numeral 20 no longer points into the hatched section of the tray side wall, which FIG. 4 labels 26; it now runs from outside the tray to the product tray as a whole, matching the assembly-numeral convention this sheet already uses for the outer shell 10, the thermal module 40 and the carrier 100. Nothing else changed: FIG. 4 still labels 26 inside the tray side wall, and the numeral table, the claims and the description are untouched. A few phrases in the same brief were tightened so the longer entry stays within the brief length limit, with every body, contact, opening, curve content and numeral on that sheet unchanged.
reasoning: The defect was a labelling convention slip, not a geometry or source problem. An assembly numeral like 20 has to reach the tray as a whole through a leader; parking it inside the tray side wall put it on the very member FIG. 4 designates 26, so one depicted feature carried two designations across the set and contradicted the statement in the description that the same numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.

I used the same phrasing pattern as the other assembly numerals on that sheet so the convention reads consistently: shell, module and carrier all get a leader from outside the container, and the tray now does too.

FIG. 4 was left alone. Numeral 26 inside the tray side wall hatching is correct for a member numeral on a sectioned part, and moving it would have broken the view that actually shows the wall, its perforations and the side supply passage.

FIG. 1 sits at its brief length ceiling, and the new entry is longer than the one it replaces, so I recovered the characters by trimming redundant words in the same brief, for example an article in the curve contents and a repeated part word in the shell and lid sentences. No geometry, contact, opening or numeral was given up to pay for it.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is nothing to cite, nothing to distinguish and no reference vocabulary to avoid. The Background carries no citation and states the problem in the inventor's own terms: the temperature spread that results when a refrigerant mass is laid against a payload, the dependence of any imposed circulation path on an alignment the packer must produce by hand, the condensate left by repeated opening of a reusable carrier, and the erasure of an excursion once the refrigerant recovers. Each states the technical problem that a specific claimed feature solves, and the solution appears in the Detailed Description in the same words the claims use, which is what a later argument would be built from. The distinguishing weight remains on lid-driven registration: the closing travel of the lid shifting the thermal module until the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so the alignment the passive circulation path depends on is produced by an act the packer cannot skip. The secondary positions are the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator, which reports the state of the refrigerant itself and survives its recovery, and the wick in a condensate channel serviced by a pull tab without opening or removing a cassette. This turn changed one leader entry in one figure brief, so no claim scope moved. Because no search was run, none of this has been measured against real references, and a search should be run before filing.

Claims 1-20 (three statutory classes, no means-plus-function, graduated dependents) each map to disclosure sentences; the optional status given to the wick features (claims 6-8, 16, 19) and the indicator (claims 9-11, 20) matches the inventor's own statement that "The wick and the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator are supported optional features." Claim 5 (cassettes removable from the frame) traces to "conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame"; claims 12 and 15 (rib meeting the channel before the lid reaches the shell edge; upwardly opening channel) follow necessarily from "the rib enters a mating channel" plus "A compressible lid gasket seals against the upper edge of the shell after registration." Title, "Not applicable" cross-reference and "Not applicable" government-support statement match input/brief.md (no priority claim, no federally sponsored research). Background is prior-art characterization only and asserts no invention matter. No drafting notes, placeholders, open questions or unresolved alternatives remain in any draft or figure file; no "by way of example"/"any closed outline" shape-justifying sentence appears in the application text; generic outlines in the figure briefs (frame body, cassette boxes, tray feet, ledge block, indicator body/stem/latch) are each marked "shown schematically" and the claims and description remain shape-neutral.

The three enlargement indications are likewise consistent: FIG-1.md draws three broken-line curves labelled FIG. 3, FIG. 4 and FIG. 5, the enclosed content of each curve matches the content of the corresponding brief, and draft/07-drawings.md describes each enlarged view as "enclosed by the broken-line curve there designated FIG. 3/4/5". Left/right handedness is mirror-consistent (FIG. 3 and FIG. 4 on the left side, FIG. 5 on the right side of FIG. 1).
6

Major, internal logic: FIG-1.md and FIG-5.md depict the tray side wall stopping short of the shell floor above the condensate channel, which leaves the side supply passage 28 open directly into the space beneath the tray. FIG-1.md and FIG-5.md, however, specify that the tray side wall stops short of the floor above the condensate channel, which leaves an unobstructed opening beneath the wall from the side supply passage into the space under the tray. This strip is the pull tab 74.' with 'A narrow strip, shown schematically, extends from one end of the absorbent body along the trough, its free end lying within the trough and clear of the absorbent body. This strip is the pull tab 74.' In figures/FIG-1.md line 7, replace ', a narrow strip rising from the right-hand appearance into the gap' with ', a narrow strip at one end of the right-hand appearance lying within the trough'. Adjust the FIG-5.md numeral note for 74 to read 'well inside the narrow strip lying in the trough beside the absorbent body.'

# FIG. 1

Schematic vertical section of an assembled cold-chain carrier, on a plane cutting both upright blocks in the module body and the groove in its top. Plain black line work, hatching on cut material, inside the drawing area.

Two thick hatched upright wall bodies joined by a thick hatched bottom body form a container open at top: the sectioned outer shell 10, its bottom the floor 12. Below its top end each wall body carries an inward-projecting block. A thick hatched slab across both top ends is the insulated lid 60, closed, a narrow rib projecting down from its underside inboard of the left top end, a compressible body between slab and each end.

Within it, a sectioned open-top box with thin hatched walls and bottom wall is the product tray 20, standing above the floor 12 on short hatched blocks, two appearing here, shown schematically, the tray feet 22, open space beneath. Its walls stand clear of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap each side, stop short of the floor 12, and carry small openings below bottom wall. One shallow trough runs around the tray, cut at both gap feet so it appears at each, and one elongated absorbent body in it appears in both, a narrow strip rising from the right-hand appearance into the gap.

Above the tray, below the lid 60, is an elongated hatched body in section, the thermal module 40, open downward at its centre, holding two upright hatched blocks, shown schematically, spaced apart. An open vertical channel runs down outboard of each block, opening through the body's outboard side below the projecting block, above the gap, and through its downward lower end over the trough. A small block is flattened between a down-facing outboard surface of the body and each inward-projecting block, the body continuing down inboard. A groove opening upward in the top surface takes the lower end of the rib.

Three broken-line curves are drawn: one upper left around the rib, groove, left wall top, compressible body, left projecting block and small block on it; one lower left around the left outboard channel opening, left gap, tray openings, tray bottom wall and space under it; one lower right around the right channel lower end and downward opening, the right tray wall lower part with its openings, right gap, bottom body, right trough, absorbent body, strip.

# FIG. 1

Schematic vertical section of an assembled cold-chain carrier, on a plane cutting both upright blocks in the module body and its top groove. Plain black line work, hatching on cut material, inside the drawing area.

Two thick hatched upright wall bodies joined by a thick hatched bottom form a container open at top: the sectioned outer shell 10, its bottom the floor 12. Each wall body carries an inward-projecting block below its top end. A thick hatched slab across both top ends is the insulated lid 60, closed, with a narrow rib projecting down inboard of the left end and a compressible body between slab and each end.

Within it, a sectioned open-top box with thin hatched walls and bottom is the product tray 20, standing above the floor 12 on short hatched blocks, two appearing here, shown schematically, the tray feet 22, open space beneath. Its walls stand clear of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap each side, and continue below the bottom wall to seat on the floor 12 inboard of the trough, so each gap reaches the space beneath the tray only through small openings in that lower portion. One shallow trough runs around the tray, cut at both gap feet so it appears at each, one elongated absorbent body in it appearing in both, a narrow strip at one end of the right-hand appearance lying within the trough.

Above the tray, below the lid 60, an elongated hatched body in section is the thermal module 40, open downward at its centre, holding two upright hatched blocks, shown schematically, spaced apart. An open vertical channel runs down outboard of each block, opening through the body's outboard side below the projecting block, above the gap, and through its downward lower end over the trough. A small block is flattened between a down-facing outboard surface of the body and each projecting block, the body continuing down inboard. A groove opening upward in the top surface takes the rib's lower end.

Three broken-line curves are drawn: upper left around the rib, groove, left wall top, compressible body, left projecting block and small block on it; lower left around the left outboard channel opening, left gap, tray openings, tray bottom wall and space under it; lower right around the right channel lower end and downward opening, right tray wall lower part with openings, right gap, bottom body, right trough, absorbent body and strip.

- FIG. 3: outside the upper left curve.

- FIG. 5: outside the lower right curve.

# FIG. 5

Enlarged view of the condensate channel region of FIG. 1 enclosed by the broken-line curve there designated FIG. 5, seen horizontally in section on the right side of the carrier. Plain black line work on white, diagonal section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

A thick hatched upright insulating wall body occupies the right portion of the drawing area, running from the upper part of the fragment down to a thick hatched horizontal bottom body that occupies the lower part and extends leftward.

In the upper left part of the drawing area, a hatched body fragment is drawn in section. An open vertical channel passes down through this fragment, bounded by hatched material to its left and right. This channel is one of the guide ducts 50. At the lower end of the channel, an opening passes through the downwardly facing bottom surface of the fragment. This opening is one of the discharge openings 76.

Below the body fragment, a thin hatched upright wall is drawn in section, spaced to the left of the inner surface of the upright wall body, its lower edge stopping short of the upwardly facing top surface of the horizontal bottom body above the trough described below. A series of small openings passes through this thin upright wall, as in FIG. 1 and FIG. 4. An open vertical space runs down between the upright wall body and the thin wall, from beneath the body fragment to the horizontal bottom body, so that the downward opening in the fragment stands above that space.

In the upwardly facing top surface of the horizontal bottom body, at the foot of the open vertical space and below the discharge opening 76, a shallow upwardly open trough is drawn in section, wider than it is deep. This trough is the condensate channel 70.

An elongated body of absorbent material lies in the trough, filling its lower part, shown schematically. This body is the absorbent wick 72. A narrow strip extends upward from its upper surface into the open vertical space, its free upper end clear of the surrounding surfaces. This strip is the pull tab 74.

- 50: inside the open vertical channel in the body fragment.
- 70: inside the trough, clear of the absorbent body.
- 72: well inside the elongated absorbent body lying in the trough.
- 74: well inside the narrow strip rising from the absorbent body.
- 76: on the opening through the bottom surface of the body fragment.

content.text:
Both findings are fixed inside the figure briefs.

- **Bypass around the perforations** — `figures/FIG-1.md` now has the tray walls continue below the bottom wall and seat on the floor 12 inboard of the trough, so each side gap reaches the space beneath the tray only through the small openings in that portion. `figures/FIG-5.md` now seats the thin tray wall's lower edge on the top surface of the bottom body immediately inboard of the trough, so the open vertical space is closed at its foot except through the small openings in that wall. Both now agree with FIG. 4, with the description, and with the path recited in claims 1, 13 and 17.
- **Pull tab in the airflow passage** — the tab no longer stands up into the side supply passage. In `figures/FIG-5.md` it is a narrow strip, shown schematically, extending from one end of the absorbent body along the trough with its free end lying within the trough, and the leader for 74 points into that strip. `figures/FIG-1.md` matches, showing the strip at one end of the right-hand appearance lying in the trough. The description keeps the tab location-neutral and was not touched.

FIG. 1 needed compression again to hold the longer flow-path wording; every body, contact, opening, curve content and numeral on that sheet is unchanged, and all seven briefs remain within the length limit. No claims, numeral-table entries or description text changed.

input.summary: Both findings are fixed and both fixes stayed in the figure briefs. FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 no longer leave a gap beneath the tray wall: the wall now continues below the tray bottom wall and seats on the floor just inboard of the trough, so each side gap reaches the space beneath the tray only through the small openings in that portion, which is the route the description and claims 1, 13 and 17 recite and the one FIG. 4 already showed. The pull tab no longer stands up inside the side supply passage; it is now a narrow strip, shown schematically, running from one end of the absorbent body along the trough with its free end lying in the trough, and the leader for numeral 74 points into that strip. FIG. 1 was compressed again to hold the longer flow-path wording within the brief length limit, with every body, contact, opening, curve content and numeral on that sheet unchanged. No claim, numeral-table entry or description sentence was touched.
reasoning: The bypass was a flow defect, not a cosmetic one. A tray wall stopping short of the floor gives descending air a free route under the skirt into the return space, so the perforations would carry little of the flow and the depicted carrier would not work the way claim 1 recites. Seating the wall on the floor inboard of the trough makes the perforations the only connection, which is what the disclosure states and what FIG. 4 already drew.

I fixed the two briefs that disagreed rather than touching FIG. 4 or the text. FIG. 4 is the enlargement that actually shows the connection and it was already correct, and the description and claims already recited the single route, so nothing in draft/ needed to move.

Seating the skirt on the floor does not disturb the disclosed suspension of the tray: the tray feet still stand on the floor and still hold the tray bottom wall above it, leaving the lower return passage, and the skirt now closes that passage's perimeter except at the perforations.

The pull tab placement was substance smuggled into a drawing. Standing the tab up into the side supply passage puts an object in the disclosed airflow path, which the inventor never said and which the description deliberately avoids by describing the tab only as accessible once the tray is out. Laying the strip along the trough keeps it reachable when the tray is lifted, adds nothing to the flow path, and it is now marked shown schematically so its form reads as a depiction convention.

FIG. 1 sits at its brief length ceiling every round, and the new flow-path clause is long, so I recovered the characters inside the same brief: the redundant open space beneath the tray, which the curve list already covers, a few articles, and three leader entries that still name a broad interior target. No geometry, contact, opening, curve content or numeral was traded away.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is nothing to cite, nothing to distinguish and no reference vocabulary to avoid. The Background carries no citation and states the problem in the inventor's own terms: the temperature spread that results when a refrigerant mass is laid against a payload, the dependence of any imposed circulation path on an alignment the packer must produce by hand, the condensate left by repeated opening of a reusable carrier, and the erasure of an excursion once the refrigerant recovers. Each states the technical problem that a specific claimed feature solves, and the solution appears in the Detailed Description in the same words the claims use, which is what a later argument would be built from. The distinguishing weight remains on lid-driven registration: the closing travel of the lid shifting the thermal module until the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so the alignment the passive circulation path depends on is produced by an act the packer cannot skip. The secondary positions are the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator, which reports the state of the refrigerant itself and survives its recovery, and the wick in a condensate channel serviced by a pull tab without opening or removing a cassette. This turn changed two figure briefs only, so no claim scope moved, and the corrected drawings now match the claimed single flow route rather than showing an alternative one. Because no search was run, none of this has been measured against real references, and a search should be run before filing.

1	# Previous review - verdict: fail
2	
3	Source ledger. The disclosure and the single USER turn in input/conversation.md are identical in substance and are the only inventor authority. They affirmatively support, element by element: the insulated outer shell 10 with floor 12, side walls 14 and upper edge; ledges 18 ("presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the shell"); the removable product tray 20 on tray feet 22 leaving lower return passage 24; tray side walls 26 spaced inward to form two side supply passages 28; perforations 30 ("passes through perforations in the product tray"); the removable thermal module 40 comprising rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes 44/46; central inlet opening 48; two downward guide ducts 50 beside the cassettes; peripheral outlet openings 54 aligned with, and in the registered position overlapping, the side supply passages; mating channel 56; resilient feet 58; insulated lid 60 with depending indexing rib 62 and compressible lid gasket 64 sealing "after registration"; condensate channel 70, absorbent wick 72, pull tab 74 and discharge openings 76 at the lower ends of the guide ducts; mechanical exposure indicator 80 with indicator stem 82, temperature-responsive latch 84 and spring 86, the latched exposed position, manual reset only after opening, and no control of airflow; the negative limitation "free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover"; and the assembly/use sequence of method claim 17. Claims 1-20 each trace: claim 5 to "conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame"; claim 4 to "two opposed phase-change cassettes" plus "divides along faces of the cassettes"; claims 12 and 15 (rib meeting the channel before the lid reaches the shell edge; upwardly opening channel) follow necessarily from "the rib enters a mating channel" combined with "A compressible lid gasket seals against the upper edge of the shell after registration"; the optional status given to claims 6-8, 16, 19 (wick) and 9-11, 20 (indicator) matches "The wick and the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator are supported optional features". Title, "Not applicable" cross-reference and "Not applicable" government-support statement match input/brief.md (no priority claim, no federally sponsored research). Background asserts prior-art characterization only and no invention matter.
4	
5	Text checks. Claims and description use the same relationships and terms throughout (registered position, overlap of peripheral outlet openings 54 with side supply passages 28, the closure-driven pressing of resilient feet 58 on ledges 18, gasket compression after registration). An open vertical channel runs down outboard of each block, opening through the body's outboard side below the projecting block, above the gap, and through its downward lower end over the trough. content.text:
The finding is fixed in the two figure briefs.

- `figures/FIG-1.md` — the tray walls now continue below the bottom wall to a lower edge closing against the floor 12 just inboard of the trough, with the tray carried by the tray feet 22, so each gap still reaches the space beneath the tray only through the small openings in that lower portion. The support path is the feet alone, as claim 1 and the description recite, and the tray is introduced as held above the floor by those feet.
- `figures/FIG-5.md` — the thin tray wall's lower edge now closes against, without bearing on, the top surface of the bottom body immediately inboard of the trough, so the vertical space is still closed at its foot except through the small openings in that wall.

The disclosed exclusive route from the side supply passage through the perforations into the lower return passage is preserved, and FIG. 4 remains as it was. Nothing in `draft/` changed: the claims, the description, the Brief Description and the numeral table are untouched. FIG. 1 needed compression again to hold the longer wording, and every body, contact, opening, curve content and numeral on that sheet is unchanged; all seven briefs remain within the length limit.

input.summary: The finding is fixed in the two figure briefs. FIG. 1 no longer seats the tray walls on the shell floor: each wall continues below the tray bottom wall to a lower edge that closes against the floor 12 just inboard of the trough, with the tray carried by the tray feet 22, and the tray is introduced as held above the floor by those feet. FIG. 5 now has the thin tray wall's lower edge closing against, without bearing on, the top surface of the bottom body immediately inboard of the trough. The disclosed exclusive air route, side supply passage through the perforations into the lower return passage, is preserved in both briefs and still matches FIG. 4, the description and claims 1, 13 and 17. Nothing in draft/ changed. FIG. 1 was compressed again to hold the longer wording within the brief length limit, with every body, contact, opening, curve content and numeral on that sheet unchanged.
reasoning: Seating the wall on the floor was a load-bearing statement, and load paths are technical substance. The inventor says the tray is suspended above the floor by feet, and claim 1 and the description attribute the support to the tray feet alone, so a drawing that rests the skirt on the floor gives the tray a second support the application never recites. Saying the edge closes against the floor keeps the geometry that blocks the bypass while leaving the feet as the only thing carrying the tray.

I kept the fix on the drawing side rather than adding a bearing relationship to the text. The text is correct as it stands, and adding an undisclosed support path to the description to match a figure would be exactly the wrong direction of authority.

FIG. 5 got the parallel treatment, with the explicit 'without bearing on' so a renderer cannot read the closed foot as the wall standing on the shell bottom. Both briefs now say the same thing about the same edge.

The reason for the closed foot is unchanged and still stated positively: each gap reaches the space beneath the tray only through the small openings in the lower portion of the wall. That is the route the disclosure gives and the one FIG. 4 draws, so the three briefs agree.

FIG. 1 sits at its length ceiling every round, so the longer clause was paid for inside the same brief: repeated left and right adjectives inside the curve list, where the curve position already fixes the side, one connective in the lid sentence, and a shortened channel phrase. No body, contact, opening, curve content or numeral was given up.

figures/FIG-1.md: the tray is introduced as held above the floor 12 by the short hatched blocks that are the tray feet 22.
figures/FIG-5.md: the thin tray wall's lower edge now closes 'against, without bearing on,' the upwardly facing top surface of the horizontal bottom body immediately inboard of the trough.

figures/FIG-1.md: wording tightened elsewhere in the brief to stay within the length limit, including the curve-content list and the module channel sentence; all bodies, contacts, openings, curve contents and numerals unchanged.
input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is nothing to cite, nothing to distinguish and no reference vocabulary to avoid. The Background carries no citation and states the problem in the inventor's own terms: the temperature spread that results when a refrigerant mass is laid against a payload, the dependence of any imposed circulation path on an alignment the packer must produce by hand, the condensate left by repeated opening of a reusable carrier, and the erasure of an excursion once the refrigerant recovers. Each states the technical problem that a specific claimed feature solves, and the solution appears in the Detailed Description in the same words the claims use, which is what a later argument would be built from. The distinguishing weight remains on lid-driven registration: the closing travel of the lid shifting the thermal module until the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so the alignment the passive circulation path depends on is produced by an act the packer cannot skip. The secondary positions are the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator, which reports the state of the refrigerant itself and survives its recovery, and the wick in a condensate channel serviced by a pull tab without opening or removing a cassette. This turn changed two figure briefs only, so no claim scope moved. Because no search was run, none of this has been measured against real references, and a search should be run before filing.

# FIG. 5

Enlarged view of the condensate channel region of FIG. 1 enclosed by the broken-line curve there designated FIG. 5, seen horizontally in section on the right side of the carrier. Plain black line work on white, diagonal section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

A thick hatched upright insulating wall body occupies the right portion of the drawing area, running from the upper part of the fragment down to a thick hatched horizontal bottom body that occupies the lower part and extends leftward.

In the upper left part of the drawing area, a hatched body fragment is drawn in section. An open vertical channel passes down through this fragment, bounded by hatched material to its left and right. This channel is one of the guide ducts 50. At the lower end of the channel, an opening passes through the downwardly facing bottom surface of the fragment. This opening is one of the discharge openings 76.

Below the body fragment, a thin hatched upright wall is drawn in section, spaced to the left of the inner surface of the upright wall body, its lower edge closing against, without bearing on, the upwardly facing top surface of the horizontal bottom body immediately inboard of the trough described below, so that the open vertical space is closed at its foot except through the small openings in the thin wall. A series of small openings passes through this thin upright wall, as in FIG. 1 and FIG. 4. An open vertical space runs down between the upright wall body and the thin wall, from beneath the body fragment to the horizontal bottom body, so that the downward opening in the fragment stands above that space.

In the upwardly facing top surface of the horizontal bottom body, at the foot of the open vertical space and below the discharge opening 76, a shallow upwardly open trough is drawn in section, wider than it is deep. This trough is the condensate channel 70.

An elongated body of absorbent material lies in the trough, filling its lower part, shown schematically. This body is the absorbent wick 72. A narrow strip, shown schematically, extends from one end of the absorbent body along the trough, its free end lying within the trough and clear of the absorbent body. This strip is the pull tab 74.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 50: inside the open vertical channel in the body fragment.
- 70: inside the trough, clear of the absorbent body.
- 72: well inside the elongated absorbent body lying in the trough.
- 74: well inside the narrow strip lying in the trough beside the absorbent body.
- 76: on the opening through the bottom surface of the body fragment.

content.text:
The finding is fixed in the two figure briefs, and nothing else changed.

- `figures/FIG-1.md` — the tray walls now continue below the bottom wall to a lower edge spaced above the floor 12 just inboard of the trough, with the tray carried by the tray feet 22 and small openings through that lower portion connecting each gap with the space beneath the tray. No floor contact and no exclusivity are asserted.
- `figures/FIG-5.md` — the thin tray wall's lower edge is now simply spaced above the top surface of the bottom body immediately inboard of the trough. The following sentence about the small openings in that wall is unchanged.

The perforated route from the side supply passage into the space beneath the tray is still drawn on both sheets and still matches FIG. 4, so the disclosed path remains visible without the briefs claiming a skirt seal. `figures/FIG-4.md`, the Brief Description, the Detailed Description, the claims and the numeral table are untouched, and all seven briefs remain within the length limit.

input.summary: The finding is fixed in the two figure briefs. FIG. 1 now has each tray wall continue below the bottom wall to a lower edge spaced above the floor 12 just inboard of the trough, with the tray carried by the tray feet 22 and small openings through that lower portion connecting each gap with the space beneath the tray, so neither floor contact nor an exclusive route is asserted. FIG. 5 now has the thin tray wall's lower edge simply spaced above the top surface of the bottom body immediately inboard of the trough, and the sentence about the small openings in that wall is unchanged. The perforated route from the side supply passage into the space beneath the tray is still drawn on both sheets and still agrees with FIG. 4. Nothing in draft/ changed, and all seven briefs remain within the length limit.
reasoning: The skirt-and-seal wording was mine, introduced in an earlier round to keep air from bypassing the perforations, and it went past what the inventor said in two ways at once: it put part of the tray against the shell floor, when the only statement about that relationship is that the tray is held clear of the floor by feet, and it declared the perforations the sole communication, when the disclosure describes the air's route without saying no other route exists. Both are structure and topology, not outline convention, so neither could be rescued by a schematic tag.

The cure keeps the drawing honest in both directions: the depending portion of the wall is still there with its openings, so the disclosed path from the side supply passage through the perforations into the lower return passage is visible, but the edge is now spaced above the floor and the brief says only that the openings connect the gap with the space beneath the tray. That is exactly what the description and claims 1, 13 and 17 recite, no more.

I left the tray feet clause in place, so the sheet still states that the feet carry the tray, which matches claim 1's tray feet standing on the floor and supporting the tray above it and removes any suggestion of a second support path.

FIG. 4 and the application text were not touched. FIG. 4 already draws the perforations as the connection it shows, and the text was never the source of the problem, so changing either to match a figure would have inverted the authority order.
Both edits shortened their briefs, so no compensating compression was needed anywhere and no geometry, contact, opening, curve content or numeral moved.
changes: figures/FIG-1.md: the tray wall clause now reads 'and continue below the bottom wall to a lower edge spaced above the floor 12 just inboard of the trough, the tray carried by the tray feet 22, small openings through that lower portion connecting each gap with the space beneath the tray', removing the floor contact and the sole-route statement.

figures/FIG-5.md: the thin tray wall's lower edge is now 'spaced above the upwardly facing top surface of the horizontal bottom body immediately inboard of the trough described below', removing the closure of the passage foot; the following sentence about the small openings through that wall is unchanged.
input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is nothing to cite, nothing to distinguish and no reference vocabulary to avoid. The Background carries no citation and states the problem in the inventor's own terms: the temperature spread that results when a refrigerant mass is laid against a payload, the dependence of any imposed circulation path on an alignment the packer must produce by hand, the condensate left by repeated opening of a reusable carrier, and the erasure of an excursion once the refrigerant recovers. Each states the technical problem that a specific claimed feature solves, and the solution appears in the Detailed Description in the same words the claims use, which is what a later argument would be built from. The distinguishing weight remains on lid-driven registration: the closing travel of the lid shifting the thermal module until the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so the alignment the passive circulation path depends on is produced by an act the packer cannot skip. The secondary positions are the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator, which reports the state of the refrigerant itself and survives its recovery, and the wick in a condensate channel serviced by a pull tab without opening or removing a cassette. This turn changed two figure briefs only, so no claim scope moved. Because no search was run, none of this has been measured against real references, and a search should be run before filing.
